home.meta.title: Aubergine: mission control for terminals and coding agents
home.meta.description: One browser dashboard to run and manage Claude Code, Codex and plain terminals side by side. See which agent needs you. Free, local, open source.
home.ld.category: Terminal and coding agent management dashboard
home.ld.requires: tmux 3.2 or newer, Node.js 22 or newer
home.hero.lead: Run Claude Code, Codex and plain terminals side by side in one browser dashboard. Aubergine has no model of its own and never asks for a key.
home.hero.after: Then aubergine start --open. For macOS, with tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer.

home.powers.title: Terminal management, rethought
home.powers.lead: The terminals you already use, with what they were missing: a place to stand side by side, a memory, and a way to tell you when they need you.
home.powers.fast.name: Improve your productivity
home.powers.fast.text: Several agents work at once, each in its own terminal. You answer the one that waits and leave the rest to run.
home.powers.dx.name: A better developer experience
home.powers.dx.text: Every terminal has a name, a color, a note and its place on the canvas. Close the browser or restart Aubergine: they are still there.
home.powers.own.name: Nothing to switch to
home.powers.own.text: Your shell, your tools, your agents and your models, as they are. Aubergine adds the canvas around them and has no model of its own.

home.agents.title: Bring your own agent
home.agents.intro: Aubergine runs ordinary terminals. It calls no model, holds no key and has no account: the command-line agents you already use, signed in as you, run in its terminals with whatever model you chose for them. What Aubergine does by itself for an agent is built for Claude Code today; any other agent can say the same things through the aubergine commands.
home.agents.claude: Start it from the New terminal menu and it says by itself when it works, waits for you or finishes; Aubergine can resume its conversations and show how it is set up.
home.agents.codex.name: Codex and ChatGPT
home.agents.codex: Codex runs in a terminal like any program, and reports through the aubergine commands once its instructions tell it to. ChatGPT in a browser is not a terminal program.
home.agents.other.name: Any other command-line agent, or a plain shell
home.agents.other: Every terminal has the aubergine command, and aubergine guide --snippet prints five lines for your agent's own instructions.
home.built.title: What else is built
home.built.intro: All of this runs on your computer today.
home.built.canvas.name: A canvas of terminals
home.built.canvas.text: Pan, zoom and arrange real terminals, click once to type, park one and bring it back later, or open one by itself in a browser tab with its details and note beside it.
home.built.waiting.name: See who is waiting
home.built.waiting.text: Busy, idle or waiting for you, on every terminal, and the “For you” list and “next waiting” take you straight to what needs a person.
home.built.queue.name: Queue and schedules
home.built.queue.text: Write a task once and let a free agent take it, or schedule it for a time of day on the days you choose.
home.built.copies.name: Working copies
home.built.copies.text: Give each agent its own copy of a repository on its own branch, so two agents never edit the same files.
home.built.projects.name: Projects
home.built.projects.text: One server, several control rooms: each project has its own canvases, queue, schedules and rules, and can be saved as a file or a template.
home.built.workflows.name: Workflows and approvals
home.built.workflows.text: Give an agent steps to follow, stop at a step that waits for a person, and watch every live run on one board.
home.built.messages.name: Messages between terminals
home.built.messages.text: Let agents talk to each other with named senders, limits and pauses, closed by default for each canvas.
home.built.api.name: API and MCP server
home.built.api.text: A local HTTP API with scoped tokens, a typed client, and an MCP server that lists only the tools a credential may use.
home.built.cli.name: A command line
home.built.cli.text: The aubergine command starts terminals, queues tasks, sets schedules, reads the board and approves runs, from any terminal on the machine.
home.built.recaps.name: Recaps and history
home.built.recaps.text: See what changed while you were away, search terminal output, and reopen past conversations from the palette.
home.trust.title: Your terminals stay yours
home.trust.local.name: Local only
home.trust.local.text: The server listens on 127.0.0.1 and checks the Host and Origin of every request; use from another device stays off until you set it up.
home.trust.outlive.name: Terminals outlive the app
home.trust.outlive.text: Every terminal is a tmux session: close the browser or restart Aubergine and your work keeps running.
home.trust.nomodel.name: No model, no key
home.trust.nomodel.text: Aubergine does not pick or call a model, and holds no key for one; your agents bring their own.
home.trust.decide.name: You decide
home.trust.decide.text: Tokens are scoped, what agents write waits for your review, and approvals are made by a person.
home.trust.more: What is protected, and what is not
home.install.title: Up and running in five minutes
home.install.intro: You need macOS with tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer. brew install tmux node gets both.
home.install.s1.title: Install
home.install.s1.text: Or use the installer, which builds from the source with pnpm.
home.install.s2.title: Start it and open your browser
home.install.s2.text: It starts the server and opens your browser, signed in.
home.install.s3.title: Take the tour
home.install.s3.text: Click Show me around on the empty canvas. It makes a Demo canvas of stand-in agents and walks you through eight short steps; aubergine demo --remove takes it away.
home.install.note: The installer changes only ~/.aubergine and one link named aubergine. It never uses sudo and never edits your shell startup files.
home.agent.title: Or have your agent install it
home.agent.intro: Paste this to the coding agent you already use. It checks what Aubergine needs, installs it, and adds a few lines to your project's instructions so that it knows how to work in an Aubergine terminal.
home.agent.note: The prompt is in English, as Aubergine is; your agent can answer in your language. It has not been run with a real agent yet, so read what yours proposes before you say yes. What an agent can do in a terminal is in the guide for agents.
home.faq.title: Questions
home.faq.what.a: A local, browser-based canvas of terminal sessions. Each terminal is a node you can arrange and use, so you can run several coding agents at once and see which one is waiting for you.
home.faq.send.q: Does Aubergine send my terminals or code anywhere?
home.faq.send.a: No. Everything runs on your own computer. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only and checks the Host and Origin of every request.
home.faq.need.q: What do I need to run Aubergine?
home.faq.need.a: macOS with tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer; the installer also needs pnpm. On Linux it has been run in containers only. On Windows it runs only inside WSL 2, which has not been tried yet: see the guide for Windows.
home.faq.byhand.q: What if I start Claude Code myself in a terminal?
home.faq.byhand.a: It works like any program: you type to it as usual. But Aubergine only knows an agent is there when it started the agent itself (New terminal, then Claude Code), because it adds a few small hooks that report what the agent is doing. Started by hand, the terminal just shows as busy running claude: it is not marked as waiting for you when it asks something, and when you start a workflow there, nothing is typed for it. Tell it yourself to run aubergine workflow status, which still works from inside, or start the agent from the New terminal menu instead.
home.faq.free.a: Yes. It is free and open source under the MIT license, and its source is on GitHub.
home.planned.title: What is planned
home.planned.line: Multiplayer, agents in the cloud, approval modes and more are planned and not built. See the roadmap.
claude.meta.title: Run Claude Code sessions side by side | Aubergine
claude.meta.description: Run several Claude Code sessions side by side. Aubergine starts them, shows which one waits for you, resumes conversations and lists past ones.
claude.title: What Aubergine does for Claude Code
claude.lead: Claude Code runs in an Aubergine terminal like any program. Started from Aubergine, it also tells the canvas what it is doing, and Aubergine can brief it, resume it and show how it is set up. This is all of it, in the order you meet it.
claude.yours: You install Claude Code and sign in to it yourself. Aubergine calls no model and holds no key: it starts the claude command you already have.
claude.start.title: Start it from the menu
claude.start.text: New terminal ▾ → Claude Code, or C while no terminal has the keyboard, starts claude in a new terminal with a settings file Aubergine writes in its own data folder. Your own Claude Code configuration is not touched.
claude.start.command: The command it starts is agents.claudeCommand in the settings, claude unless you change it; Aubergine adds its own flags at the end.
claude.start.where: Where: the menu beside New terminal, at the top of the list of terminals.
claude.state.title: See when it works, waits and finishes
claude.state.text: The hooks in that settings file tell the canvas what the agent is doing. When you submit a prompt, the prompt is added to the terminal's note log and the terminal shows working. When the agent needs you, with a permission question or because it is idle waiting for input, its line turns to the color of waiting and its title and its row say waiting for you. When it stops, it shows finished.
claude.state.more: W goes to the next terminal that waits, and Notify turns on desktop notifications for terminals that start waiting. Prompts can hold secrets: "agents": { "logPrompts": false } in config.json keeps them out of the note log.
claude.state.where: Where: the terminal's title, its row in the list, and the count beside For you at the top.
claude.byhand.title: A Claude Code you started yourself
claude.byhand.text: Typed by hand in a plain terminal, claude works like any program, but Aubergine sees only a shell busy running it: no waiting for you, and nothing is typed for it when you start a workflow there. To change that, print the hooks and add them to your own Claude Code settings by hand. They do nothing outside an Aubergine terminal.
claude.describe.title: It names itself and keeps a summary
claude.describe.text: An agent Aubergine starts is told when it begins to name its terminal after the work and keep a summary, with aubergine describe, aubergine link add and aubergine field set, and is reminded once when it stops with no name of its own or no summary. What you write yourself wins; what the agent says about the same thing waits beside it with Use this. The reminder can be switched off in Settings.
claude.describe.where: Where: the terminal's details, with its name, summary, fields and links.
claude.told.title: Workflows, tasks, recaps and messages reach it
claude.told.text: Aubergine types four fixed sentences into a terminal, and only these: that a workflow was started, that the agent was asked to write something, that you asked for a recap, and that a message waits. Each names one command for the agent to run. A sentence is typed only where an agent is seen to have the keyboard: one that Aubergine started, or one whose settings have the hooks from aubergine hooks print.
claude.told.more: In the same way, a task from the queue goes only to a terminal where such an agent is in front and free, and Claude Code on a workflow… starts a new terminal whose agent is told about the run in its first prompt.
claude.told.where: Where: Run a workflow… in the menu of a terminal's title, and Runs at the top of the page.
claude.resume.title: Resume agent
claude.resume.text: Aubergine remembers which conversation an agent terminal was in. When its shell is back at a prompt, because you exited the agent or the computer restarted, the terminal offers Resume agent, which starts the agent again in that conversation. On a terminal that is on a run, it also tells the agent about the run again.
claude.history.title: Past conversations
claude.history.text: Past conversations… lists the agent's earlier conversations in a folder: read one, open it on the canvas, or open a copy that leaves the original as it is. Type @ and some words in the palette to search them; aubergine history lists them on the command line. Nothing read is kept, and no token and no agent can read conversations through Aubergine.
claude.history.form: It reads the files Claude Code keeps. Their format is internal to Claude Code and changes between versions. After an update of the agent, names and transcripts may be thinner, and a record Aubergine cannot read is said to be so, never shown as empty.
claude.history.where: Where: the palette (⌘K), and “Past conversations in this folder…” in a terminal's details.
claude.setup.title: How it is set up
claude.setup.text: A list of what the agent's configuration files say it has been given: MCP servers, plugins, hooks, skills, permission rules and settings files, each with where it comes from, and what Aubergine added. Names only, never a value or a secret. It says how the agent is set up, not what the running agent has loaded, and it says plainly what it cannot know, such as connectors that come with your account.
claude.setup.where: Where: ⚙ on on the terminal, “What is switched on for this agent…” in the palette, and the terminal's details.
claude.tools.title: Aubergine's tools for it
claude.tools.text: Claude Code with Aubergine tools… asks first what the agent may do: None; Its own work only, with the terminal's own credential; or More…, scopes you choose, for which a token is made for that one terminal and revoked when the terminal is ended for good. The tools are aubergine mcp, passed to the agent on its launch line; its own configuration is not written.
claude.tools.where: Where: the menu beside New terminal.
claude.move.title: Bring over a Claude Code you already have open
claude.move.text: A running agent cannot be moved, but its conversation can. Open elsewhere lists your Claude Code tabs, with Fork to canvas and, for an idle agent, Stop and resume here, which asks you first. From a terminal, aubergine move does the same, and aubergine here --claude starts Claude Code on the canvas continuing that folder's last conversation.
claude.move.where: Where: Open elsewhere in the bar over the canvas, or O.
claude.copy.title: In a working copy of its own
claude.copy.text: aubergine here --copy --claude starts Claude Code in its own checkout of the repository, on its own branch, so two agents never edit the same files. The dialog for a Claude Code terminal with tools has the same choice.
claude.tried.title: What has been tried
claude.tried.text: The demo that comes with Aubergine uses stand-ins, short scripts that run the same commands and hooks a real agent does, not a real Claude Code. With a real agent, an approval, a working copy, a task from the queue and a schedule have not been tried yet.
claude.others: Another agent can say most of this through the aubergine commands: see Codex and ChatGPT.
claude.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with Anthropic. Claude and Claude Code are trademarks of Anthropic.
chatgpt.meta.title: Run Codex agents side by side in terminals | Aubergine
chatgpt.meta.description: Codex, OpenAI's command-line coding agent, runs in an Aubergine terminal like any program. What works today, and what is built only for Claude Code.
chatgpt.title: Codex and ChatGPT
chatgpt.lead: Codex is OpenAI's command-line coding agent. You install it and sign in to it yourself; in Aubergine it runs in a terminal like any other program.
chatgpt.untried.title: Not tried yet
chatgpt.untried.text: Nobody has run a real Codex in Aubergine yet. What this page says is what Aubergine does for any program in a terminal and for the aubergine commands, which is built and tested; how Codex itself behaves there has not been seen. If you try it, say how it went.
chatgpt.start.title: Start it
chatgpt.start.text: Open a terminal with New terminal, or N, and start Codex in it as you would in any terminal. Aubergine calls no model and holds no key: what Codex needs, you gave it when you signed in to it.
chatgpt.works.title: What works today
chatgpt.works.intro: Everything Aubergine does for any terminal:
chatgpt.works.side.name: Side by side
chatgpt.works.side.text: As many terminals as you like on one canvas, and canvases as tabs.
chatgpt.works.status.name: Command status
chatgpt.works.status.text: With zsh, a terminal's title shows that a command is running, and which.
chatgpt.works.keep.name: Colors, notes and fields
chatgpt.works.keep.text: Give its terminal a color, keep a note with a summary and a log, and fields such as a ticket or an owner.
chatgpt.works.park.name: Parking
chatgpt.works.park.text: × parks the terminal: it leaves the canvas and keeps running, and Parked brings it back.
chatgpt.works.focus.name: One terminal by itself
chatgpt.works.focus.text: Open the terminal in a browser tab of its own, with its details and note beside it.
chatgpt.works.copy.name: A working copy
chatgpt.works.copy.text: Shell in a folder or a working copy…, or aubergine new --copy, starts the terminal in its own checkout on its own branch, so two agents never edit the same files.
chatgpt.works.search.name: Search of output
chatgpt.works.search.text: ⌘K searches what every terminal printed, and opens the terminal scrolled back to the match.
chatgpt.report.title: What it can say through the commands
chatgpt.report.intro: Every Aubergine terminal has the aubergine command and a credential for that terminal alone. Any program there, Codex included, can use them:
chatgpt.report.attention: Marks the terminal waiting for you, with what it needs; aubergine attention working and aubergine attention done say the rest.
chatgpt.report.note: Adds a line to the terminal's note log.
chatgpt.report.describe: Names the terminal after the work and keeps its summary; aubergine link add and aubergine field set add the work's links and fields. What you wrote yourself wins.
chatgpt.report.workflow: Reads the current step of a workflow; aubergine workflow done reports it done and prints the next.
chatgpt.report.task: Proposes a task for the queue, and aubergine ask asks you for something only a person can do. Both wait on your list.
chatgpt.tell.title: How to tell it
chatgpt.tell.text: Codex does not know about Aubergine until it is told. This prints five lines to paste into the instructions your agent reads at the start of every conversation in a project; its own documentation says where they go:
chatgpt.tell.after: The lines tell it to run aubergine guide once when it is in an Aubergine terminal, and the guide says the rest. Aubergine prints the lines and never writes them into any file.
chatgpt.tell.mcp: If your agent can start an MCP server, aubergine mcp offers the same as tools; inside an Aubergine terminal it needs no address and no token for the terminal's own work.
chatgpt.only.title: Built only for Claude Code today
chatgpt.only.intro: What Aubergine does by itself for an agent is built for Claude Code. For Codex, today:
chatgpt.only.menu: It is not in the New terminal menu: you start it in a terminal yourself.
chatgpt.only.seen: Aubergine does not see it as an agent: it is not marked waiting or finished by itself, only when it runs aubergine attention.
chatgpt.only.typed: Nothing is typed for it: a workflow started on its terminal types nothing and shows the line to give it yourself, and a recap or a message is not announced to it.
chatgpt.only.queue: The queue gives it no task: a task goes only to a terminal where an agent is seen and free.
chatgpt.only.resume: There is no Resume agent, no list of past conversations, no list of how it is set up, and no dialog for Aubergine's tools.
chatgpt.only.move: aubergine move and aubergine here --claude bring over Claude Code only.
chatgpt.only.remind: It is not reminded to name its terminal or keep a summary.
chatgpt.only.more: All of it is on the Claude Code page.
chatgpt.browser.title: ChatGPT in a browser
chatgpt.browser.text: ChatGPT in a browser tab is a web page, not a program in a terminal, so it does not run on the canvas.

install.title: How to install Aubergine
install.lead: One command installs it, one starts it. About five minutes, including the tour.
install.req.title: Requirements
install.req.os: macOS. On Linux it has been run, in containers only: the npm package on Ubuntu 24.04 and the container image on Debian. Windows itself is not supported; Aubergine can run inside WSL 2, which has not been tried yet: see Install on Windows with WSL.
install.req.tools: tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer. The installer also needs pnpm.
install.req.brew: With Homebrew, one line gets both (add pnpm for the installer):
install.steps.title: Install and start
install.steps.npm: Install Aubergine from npm (needs tmux and Node.js only):
install.steps.script: Or with the installer, which also needs pnpm and builds from the source:
install.steps.start: Start it and open your browser, signed in.
install.steps.tour: Take the tour. Click Show me around in the middle of the empty canvas. It makes a canvas named “Demo” with a few stand-in agents and walks you through eight short steps. Nothing in the demo is real, and aubergine demo --remove takes it away.
install.steps.read: Prefer to read the script first? Download it, read it, and run sh install.sh --dry-run to see what it would do without changing anything.
install.changes.title: What the installer changes
install.changes.text: Two things only: the install folder (~/.aubergine, or AUBERGINE_HOME) and one link named aubergine in a folder on your PATH that you can write to. It checks everything first and changes nothing if something is missing.
install.changes.not: It does not use sudo, edit your shell startup files, install Node.js, pnpm or tmux, or touch your data folder.
install.wrong.title: If something goes wrong
install.wrong.doctor: Run aubergine doctor first. It checks the usual causes.
install.wrong.signin.see: “This browser is not signed in yet”
install.wrong.signin.do: Open the sign-in link once in that browser. aubergine open --print prints it again.
install.wrong.tmux.see: A page saying tmux is missing or too old
install.wrong.tmux.do: Install or upgrade tmux (brew install tmux), then restart the server.
install.wrong.port.see: The server will not start because the port is taken
install.wrong.path.do: The link is not on your PATH. The installer prints the one line to add to your shell's startup file.
install.wrong.badges.see: A terminal shows no status badges
install.wrong.badges.do: Status needs zsh, and a session made before an update keeps its old shell. Park it and start a new one.
install.later.title: Stop, update, uninstall
install.later.stop: Stop the server with Ctrl+C. Your terminals keep running; start the server again and reload the page to get them back.
install.later.update: Update, if you installed with npm, with npm install -g @meatgarden/aubergine@latest; if you used the installer, with aubergine update. Then restart the server.
install.later.uninstall: Uninstall with aubergine uninstall. It removes the link and, after asking, the copy the installer made. It never removes your data and never ends your terminals.
install.later.login: Start at login with aubergine service install, so you only ever open the browser.
install.next.title: Next
install.next.text: Read how to run several coding agents at once, or the guides. The full reference is in the README.

install.ld.q1: What does the Aubergine installer change?
install.ld.a1: Two things: the install folder (~/.aubergine, or AUBERGINE_HOME) and one link named aubergine on your PATH. It never uses sudo, never edits your shell startup files, and never installs Node.js, pnpm or tmux.
install.ld.a2: Installed with npm: run npm install -g @meatgarden/aubergine@latest. Installed with the installer: run aubergine update, or the installer again. Then restart the server.

install.ld.q4: Does Aubergine run on Linux or Windows?
install.ld.a4: On Linux it has been run in containers only (Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian), not yet on a Linux desktop. Windows itself is not supported; Aubergine can run inside WSL 2, the Linux that Windows provides, which has not been tried yet.

windows.meta.description: Aubergine does not run on Windows itself. It runs inside WSL 2 and is used from a Windows browser: the steps, what was tried, and fixes.
windows.title: Install Aubergine on Windows with WSL
windows.lead: Aubergine does not run on Windows itself. It runs inside WSL 2, the Linux that Windows provides, and you use it from your Windows browser.
windows.tried: What was tried. The Linux steps were run on 25 November 2026 on Ubuntu 24.04.5 (x86_64) in a container, not in WSL, with Aubergine 0.2.2 from npm: it compiled its terminal library, started, signed a browser in, ran a terminal and the demo. Installing Node.js with nvm was not run there, since Node.js 22 was already installed. Nothing on this page has been run on Windows yet. If you try it, please tell us how it went.
windows.req.title: What you need
windows.req.text: Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or newer, where WSL 2 can be installed with one command. Microsoft's page on installing WSL has the details.
windows.steps.title: Install and start
windows.steps.wsl: Install WSL. Open PowerShell as administrator, run this, and restart Windows when it is done. It installs WSL 2 with Ubuntu.
windows.steps.ubuntu: After the restart, open Ubuntu from the Start menu and choose a user name and a password for it. Every command below is typed there, in Ubuntu.
windows.steps.apt: Install what Aubergine needs: tmux, zsh and Git, and the tools that compile its terminal library, which has nothing ready-made for Linux.
windows.steps.node: Install Node.js 22. Ubuntu's own package is version 18, which is too old. One well-known way is nvm: install it, open a new Ubuntu window, then install Node.js 22.
windows.steps.nodeCheck: node -v should now say v22 or newer.
windows.steps.npm: Install Aubergine from npm. It compiles its terminal library while it installs; the whole install took 13 seconds in the trial.
windows.steps.start: Start it, and leave that window open:
windows.steps.open: Sign your browser in. In a second Ubuntu window, print the sign-in address, then open it in your browser on Windows. It signs that browser in, so treat it like a password.
windows.steps.after: After that, http://127.0.0.1:4600 works on its own in that browser. On an empty canvas, Show me around starts the tour.
windows.good.title: Good to know
windows.good.files: Keep your projects in Ubuntu, in its home folder, not under /mnt/c, where the files of Windows are reached through a slower bridge.
windows.good.agents: Install your agents inside Ubuntu, Claude Code, Codex or any other, as you would on any Linux. An agent installed in Windows is not in Aubergine's terminals.
windows.good.running: Terminals live as long as WSL runs. Closing the browser ends nothing, and Ctrl+C in the window of aubergine start stops only the server. When WSL stops, because Windows restarts or after wsl --shutdown, the terminals end, and the next aubergine start opens fresh shells in their last folders, as after a restart on a Mac.
windows.good.shell: bash or zsh. Ubuntu's shell is bash, and terminals work in it. Command status on a terminal (busy, a failed command's exit code) comes from zsh only: in the trial a zsh terminal showed exit 3 after a failed command. Make zsh your shell in Ubuntu to have it.
windows.good.missing: Not there: start at login works with macOS only (aubergine service install says so), and Open on desktop has no setting for a Windows terminal app. aubergine open could not find a browser to open in the trial; aubergine open --print always works.
windows.good.keys: Keys on Windows were chosen from what browsers document and have not been measured: see docs/keys.md. The palette always works.
windows.wrong.doctor: Run aubergine doctor in Ubuntu first. It checks Node.js, tmux, Git and the server.
windows.wrong.compile.see: Installing Aubergine fails while it compiles node-pty
windows.wrong.compile.do: The build tools are missing. Run the apt lines of step 2, then install Aubergine again.
windows.wrong.tmux.do: Ubuntu 24.04's tmux is 3.4, which is new enough: sudo apt install -y tmux, then start the server again.
windows.wrong.node.see: node -v says a version older than v22
windows.wrong.node.do: Install Node.js 22 as in step 2, open a new Ubuntu window, and install Aubergine again.
windows.wrong.address.see: The address does not open in the browser on Windows
windows.wrong.address.do: Check that aubergine start is still running in Ubuntu. Then see Microsoft's page on networking in WSL; this has not been tried with Aubergine.
windows.next.text: Stopping, updating and uninstalling are as on the install page, and everything else is in the README.

several.meta.title: How to run several coding agents at once | Aubergine
several.meta.description: Put each coding agent in its own terminal on one canvas, see which is waiting for you, hand out work from a queue, and keep each agent's changes apart.
several.title: How to run several coding agents at once
several.lead: Two agents are easy. Five are chaos: which one is stuck, which is waiting on you, which changed that file? Aubergine is built for that moment. It runs on your own computer.
several.canvas.title: 1. Give each agent a terminal on one canvas
several.canvas.text: Click New terminal, at the top of the list of terminals (or press N), and start an agent in it. Drag terminals by their title bars, resize them, and group them in frames. Related work goes on one canvas; separate pieces of work go in separate canvases (tabs) or projects, each with its own terminals, queue and schedules.
several.canvas.tmux: Every terminal is a real shell in a tmux session. Close the browser, or stop Aubergine, and your agents keep running.
several.waits.title: 2. See which agent needs you
several.waits.text: Each terminal shows whether it is busy, idle or waiting for you. That status comes from hooks in your shell and from the agents themselves, not from reading the screen. The count beside For you at the top and the W key take you straight to the next one that is waiting.
several.waits.foryou: One list, For you, gathers everything that waits on a person: questions, runs to approve, finished tasks to look at, and failed ones with the reason.
several.queue.title: 3. Hand out work from a queue
several.queue.text: Write a task once and put it in the queue. A free agent takes it when you say so, with a limit on how many run at once. For work that repeats, set a schedule. Agents can propose tasks and ask you questions, but nothing starts until you accept.
several.apart.title: 4. Keep each agent's changes apart
several.apart.text: Two agents in one folder edit the same files. Start each in its own working copy: a separate checkout on its own branch, so you can read each agent's work apart. Aubergine never merges, pushes or rebases for you.
several.steps.title: 5. Give agents steps, and decide at the gates
several.steps.text: A workflow is an ordered list of steps an agent follows, with a strip showing where it is. A step can wait for you to approve or send back. Every live run appears on one board.
several.not.title: What it does not do
several.not.model: It does not call a model or pick one for you. The agents are yours.
several.not.asyou: It does not keep an agent from doing something you could do. Agents run as you. See security for what is and is not protected.
several.not.one: It runs on one computer today. Sharing a canvas with other people and running agents in the cloud are on the roadmap, and are not built.
several.ld.q1: How do I run several coding agents at once?
several.ld.a1: Put each agent in its own terminal on an Aubergine canvas. The canvas shows which are busy, idle or waiting for you, and one list called For you gathers every question and approval.
several.ld.q2: How do I keep two agents from editing the same files?
several.ld.a2: Start each terminal in its own working copy: its own checkout of the repository on its own branch. Aubergine never merges or pushes for you.
several.ld.q3: Does it work with any coding agent?
several.ld.a3: Yes. Aubergine runs ordinary terminals, so any command-line agent can run in one. What Aubergine does by itself for an agent is built for Claude Code; any other agent can report through the aubergine commands.
copies.meta.title: Run two coding agents on one repository | Aubergine
copies.meta.description: A working copy gives each agent its own Git worktree and branch, so two agents never edit the same files and you can read each one's work apart.
copies.title: Two agents, one repository: working copies
copies.lead: Every terminal normally works in your real folder. Two agents in one repository then edit the same files, and you cannot tell whose change is whose. A working copy gives each terminal its own checkout, on its own branch.
copies.start.title: Start a terminal in a working copy
copies.start.s1: Press ▾ at the end of New terminal, at the top of the list of terminals, then Shell in a folder or a working copy….
copies.start.s2: Give the folder and choose In its own working copy. The choice is offered only where it can be had, and says why where it cannot: not a Git repository, a bare repository, or no commit yet.
copies.start.cli: From a terminal, the same thing:
copies.get.title: What you get
copies.get.text: A Git worktree in a folder Aubergine keeps under its data folder, never inside your repository, on a new branch named aubergine/<terminal name>-<six characters>. It starts from the commit your checkout is on, and the terminal starts in the same subfolder you were in. Your own checkout is never changed: not its files, not what is staged, not the branch you have checked out.
copies.get.not: Not carried over: your uncommitted changes (nothing is stashed or committed for you), and files Git ignores or does not track, such as installed dependencies and local settings. A project that needs an install step needs it again in the working copy.
copies.read.title: Read what an agent changed
copies.read.text: A terminal in a working copy shows its branch and the number of files that differ on its title bar. Click it for the changed, added and removed files, with work that is in no commit marked, and the read-only difference for any file you choose.
copies.end.title: When the terminal ends
copies.end.text: A working copy is never removed just because its terminal ended. You choose:
copies.end.branch: Keep the branch, remove the folder, when everything is committed.
copies.end.keep: Keep everything. It stays in the list, saying its terminal is gone.
copies.end.discard: Discard both, which asks a second time when the copy holds work that exists nowhere else.
copies.end.never: Aubergine never merges, pushes or rebases. What you do with a kept branch is yours.
copies.git.title: What Aubergine runs in your repository
copies.git.text: Aubergine uses the git on your PATH (2.31 or newer). For every Git command it starts, no hook runs, nothing prompts, nothing reaches the network, and submodules are not fetched. Filters named in your own Git configuration, such as large-file storage, do run, as they do for your own git status.
copies.sandbox.title: It is not a sandbox
copies.sandbox.text: A working copy keeps work apart. It does not keep an agent in: the agent runs as you and can read and change every file you can, including your own checkout. Do not rely on it to hold back an agent that does the wrong thing. See security.
copies.related: Related: run several coding agents at once · the queue and schedules (a task started on a new terminal gets a working copy of its own where the folder is in a repository).
copies.ld.howto: How to run an agent in its own working copy
copies.ld.howtoAbout: Give a terminal its own checkout and branch of a repository.
copies.ld.s1text: Press the arrow at the end of New terminal, at the top of the list of terminals, then Shell in a folder or a working copy.
copies.ld.s2: Choose In its own working copy
copies.ld.s2text: Give the folder, which must be in a Git repository with at least one commit, and choose In its own working copy.
copies.ld.s4text: Click the branch on the terminal's title bar to see changed, added and removed files and each file's difference.
copies.ld.s5text: When the terminal ends, keep the branch and remove the folder, keep everything, or discard both.
copies.ld.q1: What is a working copy in Aubergine?
copies.ld.a1: A Git worktree: a second checkout of the same repository, on its own new branch, kept in Aubergine's data folder and never inside your repository.
copies.ld.q2: Does a working copy include my uncommitted changes?
copies.ld.a2: No. They are not carried over and not touched. Commit first if the new terminal should have them.
copies.ld.q3: Does Aubergine merge or push a working copy's branch?
copies.ld.a3: No. Aubergine never merges, pushes or rebases, and never changes the branch you have checked out.
copies.ld.q4: Is a working copy a sandbox?
copies.ld.a4: No. It keeps work apart; it does not keep an agent in. The agent runs as you and can still read and change every file you can.
keep.meta.title: Keep your terminals after a restart or a crash | Aubergine
keep.meta.description: What closing the browser, restarting Aubergine and restarting the computer each do to your terminals and agents, and how to pick up where you were.
keep.title: Keep your terminals when your computer restarts
keep.lead: Closing the browser or restarting Aubergine loses nothing: every terminal keeps running. A restart of the computer ends what was running, and Aubergine brings back everything around it, so you pick up where you were instead of starting again.
keep.table.title: What happens when…
keep.table.intro: Every terminal is a shell in a tmux session, which runs apart from the browser and from Aubergine's server. What it holds is in two places: the running shell, which only tmux keeps, and everything said about the terminal, which Aubergine writes to a file in its data folder at every change.
keep.table.browser: The browser closes, crashes or updates, or you close the tab
keep.table.server: Aubergine stops, restarts or is updated
keep.table.computer: The computer crashes, restarts or installs an update
keep.row.place: Its place on the canvas, name, color, tags, fields and links
keep.row.note: Its note: the summary and the log
keep.cell.fresh: a fresh shell in the same folder
keep.cell.late: still there; a time that passed runs late
keep.table.parked: A parked terminal is kept the same way and gets a fresh shell too. A terminal whose shell had already ended stays ended, with Restart here.
keep.table.update: After an update, a terminal that was already open keeps what its shell started with (its PATH and Aubergine's shell integration) until that shell is started again. If Aubergine starts at login, run aubergine service install again after an update instead of restarting the server by hand.
keep.back.title: After a restart: back to work
keep.back.start: Start Aubergine. If it starts at login (aubergine service install, macOS only), it is running once you have logged in, and launchd starts it again if it stops. Otherwise start it and open the page:
keep.back.canvas: The canvas is as you left it. Every terminal is in its place with its name, color, tags, fields, links and note, now a fresh shell in the last folder Aubergine saw it in, or in your default folder if that one is gone. Nothing is typed or run again.
keep.back.resume: Resume your agents. Where Claude Code ran and Aubergine knows its conversation (it was started from Aubergine), the terminal's title bar offers Resume agent: it starts Claude Code again in that conversation. On a terminal that is on a run of a workflow, it also tells the agent about the run again, so it carries on from the step the run is at.
keep.back.read: See where each one stood. Details in a terminal's title shows what is known about it (a run's step and its last report, the folder, the tags), its summary, its fields and links, and its log under Log. Pointing at a terminal's name in the list shows its recap.
keep.back.history: Find a conversation that is not on the canvas. Past conversations… in the palette (⌘K), or “Past conversations in this folder…” in a terminal's details, lists Claude Code's earlier conversations in a folder and opens one on the canvas.
keep.back.other: Any other agent has no Resume agent, because Aubergine does not know its conversation: start it again in the same terminal with that agent's own way of resuming, and read the note to tell it where it stood.
keep.pic.caption: A terminal's details: a run's step and last report, the folder, tags and fields. All of it is kept through a restart of the computer; the live terminal beside it is not.
keep.lost.title: What is lost, and what to do about it
keep.lost.running: What was running ends. A build, a test run, a server or an agent in the middle of its work stops with the computer, and Aubergine starts none of them again by itself. Start them again yourself; a job that must outlast a restart belongs in something made for that, such as a service of your system.
keep.lost.work: Work Aubergine keeps track of waits for you. A run of a workflow keeps its step and every report handed in. Tasks in the queue keep their place; one that was being started at the moment the server stopped is marked failed, with a sentence, and nothing is tried again by itself. A schedule's time that passed while the server was stopped runs once, late, if it is less than six hours old (schedules.lateWithinHours), and is marked missed otherwise.
keep.lost.scrollback: The scrollback is gone. While a shell runs, tmux keeps the last 50,000 lines it printed, and the palette's search reads them. Aubergine does not record what a terminal prints, so after a restart of the computer there is nothing to bring back, and search finds only what was printed since.
keep.lost.away: “While you were away” starts again. It is kept in the server's memory, not in a file, so after the server starts it knows only what changed since then, and says so.
keep.habit.title: The habit that makes a restart cheap
keep.habit.text: The note is what survives, so have agents write to it as they go: a decision, a result, where they stopped. A Claude Code started from Aubergine has each prompt you send added to the log by itself, and is told when it begins to name its terminal and keep its summary. Any agent can do the same with these commands, which aubergine guide explains to it:
keep.habit.recap: Before you stop for the day, press Ask its agent for a recap in a terminal's details: the agent writes where it stands with aubergine recap --write, and the recap is kept with the terminal.
keep.sleep.title: Closing the laptop, sleep, and the browser
keep.sleep.sleep: Sleep is not a restart. Closing a laptop's lid usually puts it to sleep: programs pause and carry on when it wakes, and nothing in the last column of the table happens. Aubergine neither keeps the computer awake nor wakes it, so a schedule whose time passed during sleep runs late, or is missed, as above.
keep.sleep.browser: Closing the browser, a tab or its window, or a browser update that restarts it, ends nothing. Open the page again (aubergine open opens it signed in) and each terminal is drawn from tmux as it is now. A page left open reconnects by itself when the server comes back.
keep.sleep.server: Closing the window where aubergine start runs, or pressing Ctrl+C there, stops the server and nothing else: the middle column of the table.
keep.sleep.wsl: On Windows with WSL, WSL stopping, because Windows restarts or after wsl --shutdown, is a restart of the computer for Aubergine. See Windows with WSL.
keep.q.restore.q: Can Aubergine restore my terminals after a reboot?
keep.q.restore.a: Yes, all but what was running in them. Each terminal comes back in its place on the canvas with its name, color, note, tags, fields and links, as a fresh shell in its last folder. The programs that ran in it are not started again; for Claude Code, Resume agent continues the conversation.
keep.q.output.q: Does Aubergine keep my terminal output and history?
keep.q.output.a: The output, only while the shell runs: tmux keeps 50,000 lines of each terminal's scrollback, and closing the browser or restarting Aubergine loses none of it. After a restart of the computer it is gone, because Aubergine records no terminal output. The history of the commands you typed, which the up arrow brings back, is your shell's own file, kept by your shell as always.
keep.q.claude.q: Will my Claude Code conversation survive a restart?
keep.q.claude.a: The conversation, yes: Claude Code keeps it in its own files, and Aubergine remembers which one each terminal was in. After the restart, Resume agent in the terminal's title bar starts Claude Code again in that conversation. What the agent was doing at that moment stopped, and is not done again until you ask.
keep.q.macos.q: Does it work when macOS updates itself overnight?
keep.q.macos.a: An update that restarts the computer is a restart like any other: running programs end and everything else is kept. With start at login (aubergine service install), the server is running again once you log in, and the canvas is waiting. Fresh shells in their last folders were seen when a container of Aubergine was restarted; a real overnight update of macOS has not been tried.
keep.q.tmux.q: Do I need to know tmux?
keep.q.tmux.a: No. It has to be installed (3.2 or newer), and Aubergine runs it on a socket of its own with its own settings, with no status bar and no prefix key, so you never type a tmux command. Your own tmux, if you use one, is not touched.

alive.meta.title: Keep a process running after the terminal closes | Aubergine
alive.meta.description: Closing a terminal ends what runs in it. The usual answers are nohup, disown, screen and tmux. Aubergine runs every terminal in tmux for you.
alive.title: Keep a process running after you close the terminal
alive.lead: You started a build, a server or a coding agent, and closing the window would end it. In Aubergine closing the window ends nothing: every terminal runs apart from the browser, and what it printed is there when you come back.
alive.usual.title: What people usually do
alive.usual.text: Closing a terminal window ends the shell in it, and with it what that shell started. The standard ways round that:
alive.usual.nohup: nohup starts a command that ignores the hang-up sent when the terminal closes. Its output goes to a file (nohup.out unless you send it elsewhere).
alive.usual.disown: disown, in bash and zsh, lets go of a job you already started, so the shell does not pass the hang-up on to it. You cannot get back to it in a terminal afterwards.
alive.usual.mux: screen and tmux run the shell inside a server of their own. You detach, close the window, and attach again later to the same shell with its output. They are the dependable answer, and you learn their keys and commands to use them.
alive.usual.after: Aubergine is built on the last of these. It runs tmux for you, so you get its answer without its keys.
alive.does.title: What Aubergine does
alive.does.text: Every terminal in Aubergine is a shell in a tmux session of its own, on a tmux socket of Aubergine's. tmux runs apart from the browser and from Aubergine's server, so:
alive.does.browser: Closing the tab, the window or the whole browser ends nothing. Open the page again (aubergine open opens it signed in) and each terminal is drawn from tmux as it is now, with what it printed meanwhile in its scrollback.
alive.does.server: Stopping Aubergine ends nothing either. Ctrl+C where aubergine start runs, a crash of the server or an update stops the server and nothing else. Start it again and reload the page.
alive.does.park: Closing a terminal on the canvas parks it. The × in its title takes it off the canvas and its shell keeps running. Parked in the bar over the canvas lists parked terminals, and Restore brings one back.
alive.does.end: Ending a shell for good asks first. End in the parked list ends a terminal only after you say yes.
alive.does.views: Other views of it end nothing. Tab ↗ in a terminal's title opens it by itself in a browser tab, and aubergine attach <name> shows it in a window of your terminal app. Each is the same terminal, not a copy; closing that tab or window leaves it running.
alive.does.scroll: While a shell runs, tmux keeps the last 50,000 lines it printed. The wheel scrolls back through them in the terminal that has the keyboard, and the palette (⌘K) searches them.
alive.pic.caption: The list says what each terminal is doing. The parked one at the foot is off the canvas, and its shell is still running.
alive.not.title: What it does not do
alive.not.reboot: It does not survive the computer restarting. A restart, a crash of the computer, or an update that restarts it, ends every shell and what runs in it. Aubergine brings back everything around them, each terminal as a fresh shell in its last folder, and starts nothing again by itself. See Keep your terminals after a restart.
alive.not.sleep: It does not keep the computer awake. A laptop that sleeps pauses its programs, these too; they carry on when it wakes.
alive.not.service: It is not a service manager. A job that must come back by itself after a restart belongs in your system's services.
alive.not.adopt: It cannot take over a program already running elsewhere. No tool can move a running program into another terminal. aubergine here in a tab of your terminal app gives that folder a terminal on the canvas; a program running in the tab stays there, and has to be started again inside the new terminal.
alive.ssh.title: On another machine, over SSH
alive.ssh.text: Aubergine runs on your own computer: its server listens on 127.0.0.1, and its terminals are shells on that computer. If what you want kept is a process on a remote server you reach with SSH, tmux or screen on that server is still the answer.
alive.ssh.remote: Aubergine itself can run on another machine and be used from your browser, through an SSH tunnel, a private network, or a name and a proxy: Using Aubergine from elsewhere has the steps. Through an SSH tunnel, closing the SSH window that runs aubergine start stops the server, and the terminals keep running. Linux has been run in containers only, and never on a cloud machine.
alive.q.close.q: Does closing the browser stop my terminal?
alive.q.close.a: No. Every terminal is a shell in tmux, which runs apart from the browser. Close the tab, the window or the browser, open the page again, and each terminal is as it is now, still running, with what it printed meanwhile.
alive.q.ssh.q: How do I keep a process running after SSH disconnects?
alive.q.ssh.a: On the remote machine, start it inside tmux or screen, or with nohup. Aubergine keeps terminals on the computer it runs on. It can run on a remote machine too, used through an SSH tunnel or a proxy, but that has been run in containers only, never on a cloud machine.
alive.q.nohup.q: Should I use nohup or tmux?
alive.q.nohup.a: nohup suits one command whose output can go to a file. tmux suits a shell you want to come back to and type into. Aubergine gives every terminal the second, in a browser page, without tmux's keys.
alive.q.output.q: Can I see the output after I close the terminal?
alive.q.output.a: Yes, while the shell runs: tmux keeps the last 50,000 lines of each terminal, and the page shows them when you come back. Aubergine records nothing itself, so after a restart of the computer that output is gone.
alive.q.reboot.q: Will it keep running after a reboot?
alive.q.reboot.a: No. A restart of the computer ends every program. Aubergine brings each terminal back as a fresh shell in its last folder, with its place, name and note, and runs nothing again.

notify.meta.title: Know when Claude Code is done or waiting for you | Aubergine
notify.meta.description: See which Claude Code terminal is working, waiting for you or finished: a count of what waits, a key to the next one, and browser notifications.
notify.title: Know when Claude Code is done or waiting for you
notify.lead: You give Claude Code a task, turn to something else, and come back twenty minutes later to find it has waited for a yes since minute two. Aubergine shows which terminal is working, which is waiting for you and which has finished, on one page.
notify.usual.title: What people usually do
notify.usual.text: Claude Code runs hooks, commands of your own, at moments such as when it stops (Stop) or sends a notification (Notification). The usual answer is a hook in your Claude Code settings that plays a sound or shows a desktop notification. It works, and the scripts are yours to write and keep.
notify.does.title: What Aubergine does
notify.does.start: Start Claude Code from Aubergine: New terminal ▾ → Claude Code at the top of the list of terminals, or C. Aubergine starts claude with a settings file it generates in its own data folder and names on the command line. Your own Claude Code configuration is not touched. The hooks in that file tell the page what the agent is doing:
notify.does.working: when you send a prompt, the terminal shows working, and the prompt is added to its note's log;
notify.does.waiting: when the agent needs you (a permission question, or it is idle waiting for input), its line takes the color of waiting, and its title and its row in the list say waiting for you;
notify.does.finished: when it stops, the terminal shows finished.
notify.does.count: The count beside For you, at the top right of the page, is everything that waits on you, over every project: terminals with a question, and runs to approve, drafts to read and tasks proposed. Pressing it opens Runs, whose Waiting for you column is that list. A canvas's tab shows how many of its terminals wait.
notify.does.next: The next one that waits. W goes to the next terminal that is waiting for you while no terminal has the keyboard; on macOS ⌃⌘J does it from inside a terminal too. Elsewhere it is in the palette.
notify.does.desktop: Notifications from the open page. Settings → Notifications has Notify me on the desktop when a terminal starts waiting. Switched on, the page shows a notification of your browser when a terminal starts waiting or its agent has finished, unless you are looking at that terminal. The browser asks your permission once.
notify.does.rules: Rules. On the Rules tab of Runs, a rule can Notify me when a task is done, a task failed, a task needs you, something is asked of you, or a schedule fired or could not run: a notification from the open page, with a sentence of what happened.
notify.pic.caption: The list of what waits, beside For you: a stand-in agent's question first, then a step to read and a list handed in.
notify.other.title: Other agents, and a claude you typed yourself
notify.other.text: Aubergine does not read a terminal's output to guess. Any other agent, or any program, says the same by itself with aubergine attention waiting "what it needs", aubergine attention working and aubergine attention done in its terminal. aubergine guide --snippet prints five lines for the file your agent reads at the start of a conversation; they tell it to run aubergine guide, which explains these commands.
notify.other.typed: A Claude Code you started by typing claude in a plain terminal is a shell busy with a program to Aubergine: no waiting for you. Start it from the menu instead, or add the hooks that aubergine hooks print prints to your own settings by hand; they do nothing outside an Aubergine terminal.
notify.not.title: What it does not do
notify.not.sound: No sound of its own. Aubergine plays none. A notification makes a sound only if your browser or your system does that for notifications.
notify.not.closed: Nothing while no page is open. Notifications come from an Aubergine page open in your browser; the server sends none by itself. With every page closed, the terminal still says waiting for you, and the count is there when you open the page.
notify.not.phone: No push to a phone. There is no app and no push service. A phone's browser can be paired to open the same page; see Check on your agents from your phone, which has not been tried on a real phone.
notify.not.tried: What was checked. The browser tests check the notifications against a stand-in for the browser's own. How a real one looks, and whether it is shown at all, is up to your browser and your system's settings for it.
notify.q.done.q: How do I get a notification when Claude Code finishes?
notify.q.done.a: Start Claude Code from Aubergine, then switch on Notify me on the desktop when a terminal starts waiting under Settings → Notifications. The open page then shows a browser notification when a terminal starts waiting for you or its agent has finished. Without a notification, the terminal says finished.
notify.q.sound.q: Can Claude Code play a sound when it needs input?
notify.q.sound.a: Aubergine plays no sound. A notification sounds if your browser or system makes it sound. A hook of your own in your Claude Code settings can play one; Aubergine never writes to those settings.
notify.q.several.q: How do I see which Claude Code session is waiting when I run several?
notify.q.several.a: In Aubergine the waiting terminal's line and its state are in the color of waiting, its row in the list says waiting for you, and the count beside For you says how many things wait. W goes to the next one.
notify.q.closed.q: Do I get notified when the browser is closed?
notify.q.closed.a: No. Notifications come from an open Aubergine page. The state is kept, so the terminals that wait are marked when you open the page again.
notify.q.other.q: Does it work with agents other than Claude Code?
notify.q.other.a: Not by itself: the hooks are built for Claude Code. Any other agent can report the same with aubergine attention waiting, working and done when its own instructions tell it to; aubergine guide --snippet prints the lines for those instructions.

resume.meta.title: Resume a Claude Code session after a restart | Aubergine
resume.meta.description: claude --continue and --resume need the right folder. Aubergine remembers each terminal's conversation, offers Resume agent and lists past ones.
resume.title: Resume a Claude Code conversation after a restart
resume.lead: The computer restarted, or you closed the terminal, and Claude Code's conversation looks gone. Claude Code keeps it. Aubergine remembers which conversation each terminal was in and brings it back with one button.
resume.usual.title: What people usually do
resume.usual.text: In a terminal, in the folder the conversation was in: claude --continue carries on the most recent conversation there, and claude --resume lets you pick one from a list, or takes a conversation's ID. The catch is the folder and the choice: with several agents in one folder, the most recent is not always the one you meant.
resume.does.title: What Aubergine does
resume.does.remember: A terminal remembers its conversation. When Claude Code was started from Aubergine (New terminal ▾ → Claude Code, or C), its hooks tell Aubergine which conversation it is in, and Aubergine keeps that ID with the terminal.
resume.does.button: Resume agent is offered in the terminal's title bar once its shell is back at a prompt: you exited the agent, or the computer restarted and the terminal came back as a fresh shell in its last folder. It starts Claude Code again with --resume and that ID, with the launch command from your settings (agents.claudeCommand, claude by default).
resume.does.run: On a run of a workflow, Resume agent also tells the agent about the run again, so it carries on from the step the run is at.
resume.does.past: Past conversations… in the palette (⌘K), or “Past conversations in this folder…” in a terminal's details, lists Claude Code's earlier conversations in a folder: the name or the first thing you said, when it was last active, how many times you spoke, and whether a terminal on a canvas is on it now. Read shows it, read only. Open on the canvas starts a new terminal in that folder resumed in it, and Open a copy starts a branch of it and leaves the original as it is. If a terminal is on that conversation already, you are asked first.
resume.does.search: Search. Type @ and some words in the palette to search past conversations in the folders of the terminals on your canvases. It reads the records when you ask, within limits, and says when it was cut short. On the command line, aubergine history lists them and aubergine history open <id> opens one.
resume.does.stood: Where it stood. The terminal's note keeps its summary and a log, and each prompt you send is added to the log. Ask its agent for a recap in its details has the agent write where it stands with aubergine recap --write, kept with the terminal. When you come back after more than 30 minutes, While you were away lists what changed meanwhile.
resume.pic.caption: A terminal's details: its run's step and last report, its folder and its fields. They are kept with the terminal, ready for when its agent is resumed.
resume.outside.title: A conversation in a terminal outside Aubergine
resume.outside.text: In a tab of your terminal app, exit the agent, then run aubergine here --claude in the same folder: a new terminal on the canvas starts Claude Code with --continue, now with its state shown. aubergine move lists your Claude Code tabs and starts a copy of each conversation on the canvas; with --stop it asks an idle agent to exit first, after you confirm.
resume.not.title: What it does not do
resume.not.format: It reads Claude Code's own records, in a form that is not Aubergine's. Claude Code calls the form of those files internal, and it changes between versions. Resuming uses Claude Code's own --resume with the ID; names, counts and transcripts are Aubergine's reading of the files, and may be missing or thinner after an update of Claude Code. A record it cannot read is said to be so, not shown as an empty conversation.
resume.not.store: Nothing is copied or kept. A list, a transcript or a search is read when you ask and dropped when you close it. Aubergine never changes, renames or deletes a conversation, and no agent or token can read conversations through it.
resume.not.work: The work in progress is not redone. What the agent was doing when it stopped is not started again until you ask it.
resume.not.other: No Resume agent for another agent. Aubergine does not know another agent's conversation, and lists no past conversations for it. Start it again in the same terminal with that agent's own way of resuming, and read the note to tell it where it stood.
resume.not.typed: A claude you typed yourself is not remembered, unless you added the hooks that aubergine hooks print prints to your own Claude Code settings.
resume.not.tried: What was checked. The reading of conversation records is tested against made-up records. It has not been checked against every version of Claude Code.
resume.q.closed.q: How do I resume a Claude Code session after closing the terminal?
resume.q.closed.a: In the same folder, claude --continue takes the most recent conversation and claude --resume lets you choose. In Aubergine, closing the browser ends nothing, and a terminal whose agent you exited offers Resume agent in its title bar.
resume.q.reboot.q: How do I resume a Claude Code conversation after a reboot?
resume.q.reboot.a: After a restart each Aubergine terminal comes back as a fresh shell in its last folder. Where Claude Code was started from Aubergine, Resume agent in the title bar starts it again in the conversation that terminal was in.
resume.q.find.q: How do I find an old Claude Code conversation?
resume.q.find.a: Past conversations… in the palette lists them for a folder, with a read-only transcript; @ and some words in the palette searches them. Only what Claude Code still keeps is listed.
resume.q.diff.q: What is the difference between claude --continue and claude --resume?
resume.q.diff.a: --continue carries on the most recent conversation in the folder; --resume takes the one you choose, or an ID. Resume agent uses --resume with the ID the terminal remembered, so it does not depend on which conversation was most recent.
resume.q.two.q: Can two terminals continue the same Claude Code conversation?
resume.q.two.a: Aubergine does not open one twice without asking: two agents in one conversation lose each other's messages. You are offered the terminal already on it, or a copy, which branches the conversation.

many.meta.title: Too many terminal tabs? Find the right one | Aubergine
many.meta.description: Too many terminal tabs, all named zsh? Aubergine puts every terminal on a canvas and in one list, with its state, filters, tags and output search.
many.title: Find the right terminal when you have too many
many.lead: Twenty tabs, most of them named zsh, three of them running an agent, one of those waiting for you. Aubergine puts every terminal on a canvas and in one list that says what each is doing, so you find a terminal by what it is, not by where you left it.
many.usual.title: What people usually do
many.usual.text: Name the tabs or windows (most terminal apps let you), split windows into panes, use named tmux sessions and windows, or let a tiling window manager place them. These help you place terminals; finding the one that needs you still means looking.
many.does.title: What Aubergine does
many.does.canvas: A canvas. Terminals side by side, each live. Drag one by its title, resize it from its edges, double-click the title to rename it. The dot in a title gives it a color; a frame (New terminal ▾ → Frame, or G) groups terminals under a label and moves them together.
many.does.canvases: Canvases and projects. Several canvases, shown as tabs, one list or a column at the left, each with its own address. A project holds its own canvases, terminals, queue and list of what waits; the switcher at the top left goes between projects.
many.does.list: One list of every terminal. The side panel's Terminals lists each one with its state in words (working, waiting for you, finished, a command that failed), the step of its run and when it was last active, for this canvas or all canvases. The field at its top finds a terminal by name, folder, command, note or tags.
many.does.filter: Filter holds the filters (waiting for me, busy, unread, has an agent, parked, tags) and how the list is laid out: by canvas, or one flat list in canvas order, by last updated, by last typed in, or by name.
many.does.goto: Go to… over the canvas, or ⌘K, is the palette: type part of a name, folder, command or note. Its Terminal output section searches what terminals printed (the last 50,000 lines tmux keeps for each), and a result opens that terminal scrolled back to it.
many.does.map: The map, its button beside Go to…, shows the whole canvas small and pans it. Fit (F) shows everything at once.
many.does.about: What a terminal is for. Each has a note beside it (a summary and a log), and in its details tags, links, and fields such as Ticket: DEMO-12. An agent can write its own terminal's name, summary and fields with the aubergine commands.
many.does.alone: One terminal by itself. Tab ↗ in its title opens it in a browser tab of its own, at /t/<terminal>, with its details and note a button away.
many.does.keys: Tab and Shift+Tab walk the terminals in the order the list shows them, and W goes to the next one that waits for you.
many.not.title: What it does not do
many.not.arrange: It does not arrange things for you. A terminal stands where you put it (a new one goes into free space near the middle of the view), and keeps the name you or its agent gave it.
many.not.number: It promises no number. Only the canvas you look at keeps live terminals: zoomed far out a terminal shows a picture of its screen, and off screen it costs the page nothing. Each terminal is still a shell on your computer. The list is tested with 1,000 terminals in a unit test (listing, filtering and drawing only a screenful), and a script fills three canvases with 90 terminals for judging by hand. Neither is a promise about your computer.
many.not.others: Your terminal app's tabs are not shown. Open elsewhere (O) lists the terminals open there and brings them over one at a time, as a new terminal in the same folder. A program running in a tab stays in that tab.
many.q.organize.q: How do I organize lots of terminal windows?
many.q.organize.a: In Aubergine: one canvas per piece of work, terminals side by side with names and colors, frames around those that belong together, and one list of all of them with what each is doing.
many.q.which.q: How do I find which terminal is running a command?
many.q.which.a: The field over the list matches a terminal's name, folder, command, note and tags, and the palette (⌘K) does the same over every canvas. A terminal's title shows what it runs.
many.q.search.q: Can I search the output of all my terminals?
many.q.search.a: Yes, of those still running: the palette's Terminal output section reads each terminal's history when you search, parked ones included, as far back as tmux keeps (50,000 lines). Nothing is indexed or recorded.
many.q.count.q: How many terminals can Aubergine handle?
many.q.count.a: There is no set limit. The list is tested with 1,000 terminals and three canvases of 90 have been looked at by hand; each terminal is still a shell, so what your computer can run decides.
many.q.name.q: Can I name and color my terminals?
many.q.name.a: Yes. Double-click a terminal's title to rename it, and use the dot in its title for one of thirteen colors or your own. Canvases have names and colors too.

tmux.meta.title: tmux without learning tmux | Aubergine
tmux.meta.description: Shells that outlive the window, with no prefix key and no .tmux.conf. Aubergine runs tmux for you; the wheel, copy and paste work as usual.
tmux.title: tmux without learning tmux
tmux.lead: tmux keeps your shells running when the window closes. It also asks you to learn a prefix key, copy mode and a configuration file. Aubergine runs tmux for you, and you use each terminal in a browser page as you would any terminal.
tmux.who.title: Who it is for
tmux.who: For people who want what tmux gives, shells that outlive the window, without its keys and its configuration. If you already live in tmux, keep it: Aubergine leaves your tmux alone.
tmux.usual.title: What people usually do
tmux.usual.text: Learn tmux: a prefix key (Ctrl+B unless you change it) before each command, tmux attach to come back, and lines in ~/.tmux.conf for the mouse and the clipboard. Or screen, an older tool of the same kind. Here is what each everyday thing is in tmux by default and in Aubergine:
tmux.row.name: Name one
tmux.cell.several.here: Terminals side by side on a canvas
tmux.does.title: What Aubergine does
tmux.does.own: Its own socket and its own configuration. Aubergine starts tmux on a socket of its own, named aubergine, with a configuration file of its own instead of yours: no status line, no prefix key, the mouse on, 50,000 lines of history. Each terminal is one tmux session with one shell, your login shell. Your own tmux, its sessions and your ~/.tmux.conf are not touched.
tmux.does.scroll: The wheel scrolls back through the terminal that has the keyboard; anywhere else on the canvas it zooms.
tmux.does.copy: Select with the mouse and it is copied to your clipboard when you let go: tmux hands what was selected to the page with OSC 52, the escape sequence terminals use for the clipboard, and the page puts it there. Paste with ⌘V (Ctrl+Shift+V outside macOS). A paste of several lines is bracketed, so a shell does not run it line by line.
tmux.does.size: Resize by dragging a terminal's edges on the canvas, and the shell gets its new size. A terminal open in two places at once has one size, set by the view you typed into last.
tmux.does.still: It is still tmux underneath. aubergine attach <name> shows a terminal in a window of your terminal app, and Open on desktop in a terminal's menu does that for you (on macOS in Terminal or iTerm; on Linux with a command line you set). With the server stopped, tmux -L aubergine ls and tmux -L aubergine attach -t <id> still reach every shell.
tmux.need.title: What you need
tmux.need.text: tmux 3.2 or newer, installed by you: brew install tmux on macOS, your system's package on Linux. Aubergine does not install it, and shows a page saying so when it is missing or older. A terminal's title shows the command running and how the last one ended with zsh; other shells run without that.
tmux.not.title: What it is not
tmux.not.ssh: Not tmux on a remote server. Aubergine's tmux runs on the computer its server runs on. For a shell on a machine you reach with SSH, tmux on that machine is still the tool. Aubergine itself can run on another machine (Using Aubergine from elsewhere); that has been run in containers only.
tmux.not.yours: Your own tmux sessions are not shown. The canvas holds Aubergine's terminals only. aubergine scan lists the interactive shells open on this computer outside Aubergine, and aubergine import or aubergine here gives one a new terminal on the canvas in the same folder; a program running in the old one stays there. The lines that aubergine shell-hook print offers for your .zshrc do nothing inside tmux.
tmux.not.keys: No tmux keys and no panes. There is no prefix key, and your own tmux bindings do not apply. While a terminal has the keyboard every key goes to the program in it, except a few chords chosen so that no shell, editor or tmux needs them.
tmux.not.windows: Not on Windows itself. It needs tmux and a Unix shell; on Windows it runs inside WSL 2. See Windows with WSL.
tmux.q.shortcuts.q: Can I use tmux without learning the shortcuts?
tmux.q.shortcuts.a: Yes. Aubergine runs tmux with no prefix key and no status line, so you never type a tmux command: close the tab to leave, open the page to come back, scroll with the wheel, copy by selecting.
tmux.q.config.q: Does Aubergine change my tmux configuration?
tmux.q.config.a: No. It runs tmux on a socket of its own, aubergine, with a configuration file of its own. Your tmux server, its sessions and your ~/.tmux.conf are left as they are.
tmux.q.copy.q: How do I scroll and copy in Aubergine's terminals?
tmux.q.copy.a: Click a terminal to give it the keyboard, then use the wheel to scroll back. Select text with the mouse: it is on your clipboard when you let go. Paste with ⌘V, or Ctrl+Shift+V outside macOS.
tmux.q.attach.q: Can I attach to an Aubergine terminal from my own terminal app?
tmux.q.attach.a: Yes: aubergine attach <name>, or Open on desktop in the terminal's menu. It is the same terminal in both places; what you type in one shows in the other.
tmux.q.ssh.q: Can Aubergine replace tmux on a server I SSH into?
tmux.q.ssh.a: Not as such: its terminals are on the machine its server runs on. It can run on a server and be used from your browser through an SSH tunnel or a proxy, which has been run in containers only, never on a cloud machine.
