phone.meta.title: Check on your coding agents from your phone | Aubergine
phone.meta.description: Reach Aubergine from a phone's browser: HTTPS on your own computer, each device paired with a one-time code. Run once on one Mac; not tried on a phone.
phone.title: Check on your agents from your phone
phone.lead: You left three agents working and went out. Is one of them waiting for a yes? Once you set it up, Aubergine can be opened in a phone's browser: the same page and the same terminals, each device paired with a one-time code.
phone.tried: What has been tried, and what not. Use from another device was run once, on 22 November 2026: the container setup in docker/ on one Mac, with Caddy in front under https://aubergine.localhost and Chromium on the same Mac, which paired with a code, typed into terminals and was signed out when its device was revoked. Not tried: a real phone, scanning the QR code with one, a real name with a public certificate, a private network, a cloud machine, two separate machines. The page is not laid out for a phone's width. The rest comes from the code and its tests. Take this as something to try, not something promised.
phone.usual.title: What people usually do
phone.usual.text: An SSH app on the phone, into the computer, then tmux attach to the session an agent runs in. Or a tunnel, or a private network that makes the computer reachable from the phone. Both work; checking several agents that way means attaching to each in turn on a small keyboard.
phone.does.title: What Aubergine does
phone.does.off: It is off by default, and stays bound to this computer. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, and that does not change. Something on the same computer carries HTTPS to it under a name, such as a private network's own HTTPS serving or a web server like Caddy. Aubergine never speaks HTTPS itself.
phone.does.address: You write the address in the settings. It goes under access.addresses in config.json, and is read when the server starts; no page or program can change it. aubergine doctor lists the addresses and what is wrong with any.
phone.does.pair: Each device is paired with a one-time code. aubergine device add --name "Phone" at the computer, or Settings → Devices → Add a device in a signed-in browser, shows a code and, for each address, a QR code of a link with the code in it. Scan it, open the link, or type the code on the phone's sign-in page. A code works once, for three minutes.
phone.does.revoke: A device can be revoked. aubergine device revoke "Phone", or Revoke… under Settings → Devices, signs it out at once and closes what it has open. A device not used for 90 days stops working.
phone.does.owner: A paired device is the whole owner. It can do everything you can at the computer: every terminal, so a shell on that computer as you. Pair only browsers you would hand your keyboard to. What acts on the computer's own desktop, Open on desktop, is left out of the page there and refused.
phone.see.title: What you would see
phone.see.text: The same page as at the computer: the canvas and its terminals, the count beside For you and the list of what waits, and one terminal by itself at /t/<terminal> with its details and its note. It is not laid out for a phone; it works as it does in a narrow window.
phone.see.steps: The three ways to set it up (an SSH tunnel, a private network, a name of your own and a proxy), pairing, and what to do when it does not work are in Using Aubergine from elsewhere. An SSH tunnel needs no settings at all, and is awkward on a phone.
phone.not.title: What it does not do
phone.not.push: No app and no push. It is a page in the phone's browser, up to date while it is open. Nothing is sent to a phone whose page is closed.
phone.not.awake: No answer from a sleeping laptop. With the server on a laptop, the phone reaches it only while the laptop is awake. A machine that stays on is the other choice.
phone.not.public: No protection for an address anyone can open. Without a code nobody gets in, and codes are hard to guess, but strangers would be guessing at a shell. Put a private network, or your organisation's own sign-in, in front of it, and never use a private network's mode that publishes a machine to the whole internet.
phone.not.layout: No layout for a phone. The page works as in a narrow window. Reading a terminal and answering a question work that way; arranging a canvas is for a larger screen.
phone.q.check.q: Can I check on my coding agents from my phone?
phone.q.check.a: Once Aubergine is reachable over HTTPS and the phone's browser is paired, the phone shows the same page: which terminal waits, the list of what waits, and each terminal. It has been run with a browser on the same Mac, not yet on a real phone.
phone.q.pair.q: How do I pair my phone with Aubergine?
phone.q.pair.a: Run aubergine device add --name "Phone" at the computer, or use Settings → Devices → Add a device. Scan the QR code, open the link, or type the code on the phone's sign-in page within three minutes.
phone.q.lost.q: What if I lose my phone?
phone.q.lost.a: Revoke it at the computer: aubergine device revoke "Phone", or Revoke… under Settings → Devices. It is signed out at once, and what it had open is closed.
phone.q.internet.q: Is it safe to put Aubergine on the internet?
phone.q.internet.a: An address anyone can open puts the sign-in in front of everyone, and a paired device has a shell on your computer. Prefer a private network, or your organisation's own sign-in in front of the address.
phone.q.asleep.q: Does it work when my laptop is asleep?
phone.q.asleep.a: No. A sleeping laptop answers nothing, and its terminals pause until it wakes. To reach agents at any hour, the server has to run on a machine that stays awake.

queue.meta.title: A task queue and schedules for coding agents | Aubergine
queue.meta.description: Write a task once and let a free agent take it, see everything that waits on you in one list, and run tasks at set times with schedules.
queue.title: The queue, “For you” and schedules
queue.lead: Two lists that feed each other: the queue holds work for agents, and For you holds everything that waits on a person. Schedules add tasks to the queue at set times.
queue.queue.title: The queue
queue.queue.text: Open Runs at the top of the page (or press Q) and click Add task. A task has a title, what to do, and optionally a folder, a workflow, and who may take it. By default any terminal where an agent is free may take it; you can name one terminal, or have a new agent terminal started for it, in a working copy of its own where the folder is in a repository.
queue.queue.next: Start next starts the first task that someone can take now. A plain shell is never given a task.
queue.queue.limit: At most N at once, three unless you change it. Hold stops new starts and touches nothing that is running.
queue.queue.itself: Start by itself is off until you switch it on. Nothing checks on a timer.
queue.queue.order: The order is yours: drag a task, or use the arrow keys.
queue.queue.follows: A task follows its run: needs you while a run waits for approval, done when it finishes, failed with a sentence when it stops. Nothing is tried again by itself.
queue.pic.caption: For you on the Runs page: a question, a draft to read and a list handed in, each with what it is.
queue.pic.alt: The Waiting for you column of the Runs page: a box to add a to-do, then a stand-in agent's question, a draft to read and a list handed in.
queue.foryou.title: For you
queue.foryou.text: Terminals with a question, runs to approve or blocked, drafts and installs to read, tasks proposed for the queue, finished and failed tasks, lists an agent handed in, and working copies whose terminal is gone. The count beside For you at the top and “next waiting” are the same list. Most of it is gathered, not written: an item goes when the thing itself is done.
queue.foryou.propose: An agent that finds work it should not do now can propose a task, and one that needs a person can ask you:
queue.foryou.land: Both land on your list. A proposal starts nothing until you accept it.
queue.schedules.title: Schedules
queue.schedules.text: A schedule is a time of day, days of the week, something to run and somewhere to run it. When its time comes it adds one task to the queue, and the queue starts it. Under Schedules on the Runs page, or aubergine schedule. The time is on this computer's clock; there are no expressions and nothing more often than once a day.
queue.schedules.run: aubergine schedule run tries a schedule now.
queue.plan.title: When things are not as planned
queue.plan.awake: The computer must be awake and Aubergine running. A time that passed while it slept runs once when it is back, marked late, if it is under six hours old. Otherwise it is marked missed.
queue.plan.skipped: While the previous task of a schedule still waits or is at work, it does not add another, and says it was skipped.
queue.plan.gone: If something it names is gone (the terminal, the step, the canvas), it does not run, and one item on your list says so.
queue.rules.title: Rules
queue.rules.text: Under Rules, you can say “when a task is done, failed or needs me, or a schedule fired or was missed, then notify me or run a saved step”. Rules are yours alone to write: no program and no agent can add or change one, and a rule cannot set itself off.
queue.rules.nothing: Aubergine calls no model and holds no credential for any app. A task or schedule only starts a run; the agent that takes it does the work with its own tools.
queue.related: Related: working copies · run several coding agents at once
queue.ld.headline: The queue, the For you list and schedules
queue.ld.q1: What is the queue in Aubergine?
queue.ld.a1: Work for agents. You write a task once, with a title, details and optionally a folder, a workflow and who may take it. A free agent takes it when you say so.
queue.ld.q2: What is the For you list?
queue.ld.a2: Everything that waits on a person in one place: terminals with a question, runs to approve, drafts to read, finished and failed tasks, and lists agents handed in.
queue.ld.q3: Can an agent start work on its own?
queue.ld.a3: An agent can propose a task or ask you something, but a proposal starts nothing until you accept it.
queue.ld.q4: What happens to a schedule when my computer is asleep?
queue.ld.a4: Nothing wakes the computer. A time that passed while it slept runs once when it is back, marked late, if it is less than six hours old. Older than that it is marked missed.
security.meta.title: Security and privacy | Aubergine
security.meta.description: Aubergine runs only on your computer, listens on 127.0.0.1, checks every request, scopes every token, and says plainly what it does not protect against.
security.title: Security and privacy
security.lead: What Aubergine does to protect your terminals, and, just as important, what it does not. The short version: it is local, it asks before it acts for an agent, and agents still run as you.
security.local.title: Everything stays on your computer
security.local.bind: The server binds to 127.0.0.1 only. Every request, and every WebSocket upgrade, has its Host and Origin checked, and the browser must hold an access cookie.
security.local.elsewhere: Using Aubergine from another device is off until you set it up: something on the same computer carries HTTPS to it under a name you write in the settings, and each browser is paired with a one-time code and can be revoked. A paired device can do everything the owner can. Using Aubergine from elsewhere says how.
security.local.network: Aubergine calls no model and starts no network request of its own, with two exceptions: fetching a library source (a Git address) when you ask for it, and asking your own gh tool, where it is installed and signed in, for the pull request of a terminal's branch.
security.local.notify: Desktop notifications come from the open page. Nothing leaves your computer.
security.callers.title: Three kinds of caller, each judged on its own
security.callers.text: Every request is checked against what the caller may do before anything is looked up, so a caller without the right learns nothing from the answer. The callers are you (signed in to the browser), an agent's session, and an API token.
security.callers.scopes: API tokens have scopes. The secret is shown once and never stored; only a hash is kept. Calls made with a token go into an activity log: who, what and how it ended, never the secret and never what was sent.
security.callers.never: Some things no token can ever do: create or revoke tokens, read the activity log, change settings, and anything about terminals outside Aubergine.
security.callers.terminal: Terminal access is two separate scopes, one to read and one to type, each limited to the sessions you choose. You can mark a terminal people only to close it to every token.
security.callers.agent: An agent's own credential is narrow. It can set its own attention, add to its own notes, report its own status and read the run it is on. It cannot reach other terminals, canvases or tokens.
security.alone.title: What an agent cannot do alone
security.alone.draft: What an agent or program writes (a workflow, a step) arrives as a draft you review. Accepting is yours alone.
security.alone.person: A step that waits for a person can be approved or sent back only by a person. Rules, schedules and the demo are yours alone.
security.alone.typed: Aubergine types only a few fixed sentences into an agent's terminal, such as “read your next step”. Nothing you stored, and nothing an agent wrote, is typed.
security.alone.library: Installing from a library needs you to accept the exact content you were shown.
security.not.title: What this does not protect against
security.not.asyou: Agents run as you. An agent in a terminal can do anything you can do in that terminal, including running commands, reading files and, if it chooses, using your own browser session.
security.not.approvals: Approvals are not a lock. An agent that runs as you can decide as you. The decision is recorded, not prevented.
security.not.copies: Working copies are not a sandbox. They keep work apart and do not keep an agent in.
security.not.review: The review screen is the control for library items. An item is instructions an agent will follow with everything that agent may do. Do not install what you have not read.
security.not.guide: The guide for agents is advice, not a lock.
security.installer.title: The installer
security.installer.text: It changes two things: its own folder and one link named aubergine. No sudo, no edits to your shell startup files, and it never touches your data folder. aubergine uninstall removes only what it made.
security.report.title: Report a problem
security.report.text: Open an issue on GitHub. Do not put secrets or tokens in it.
security.related: Related: working copies · FAQ · roadmap (approval modes and command policy are planned, not built)
security.ld.q1: Does Aubergine send my terminals or code anywhere?
security.ld.a1: No. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so it is reachable from your computer and nowhere else until you set up use from another device. Aubergine calls no model and fetches nothing unless you add a library source yourself; where your own gh tool is installed, it asks it for the pull request of a terminal's branch.
security.ld.q2: Can an agent change Aubergine's settings or make itself a token?
security.ld.a2: No. Creating tokens, changing settings, reading the activity log and anything about terminals outside Aubergine are never allowed to a token, whatever scopes it has.
security.ld.q3: Does an approval stop the owner's own agent from approving itself?
security.ld.a3: No. An agent that runs as you can act as you. Approvals are recorded, not enforced against your own agent.
security.ld.a4: No. They keep work apart but do not keep an agent in. Agents run as you.
roadmap.meta.title: Roadmap: what is planned for Aubergine | Aubergine
roadmap.meta.description: What Aubergine does today and what is planned and not built yet: multiplayer, sandboxed cloud agents, approval modes, quality gates, an SDK and more.
roadmap.title: Roadmap
roadmap.lead: None of this exists today. It is where we want to go, and the order may change. For what is built now, see the guides.
roadmap.note: Planned work is a direction, not a promise. The repository shows what is shipped.
roadmap.teams.title: Teams and connections
roadmap.teams.sub: People working together, and agents reached from the tools you already use.
roadmap.teams.multiplayer.name: Multiplayer
roadmap.teams.multiplayer.text: Share a canvas with other people and their agents. See who is working where, hand a waiting agent to a teammate, and answer together.
roadmap.teams.chat.name: Chat interface
roadmap.teams.chat.text: Ask agents and answer their questions from a team chat app, with the same identity and settings as in the browser.
roadmap.teams.tickets.name: Tickets and pull requests
roadmap.teams.tickets.text: Turn an issue into a queued task, open a pull request from a working copy, and report the result back to the ticket.
roadmap.teams.watches.name: Watches, webhooks and triage
roadmap.teams.watches.text: Start work when something happens: a failed CI job, an alert, a watched change or a call from another service. Rules decide what becomes a task.
roadmap.teams.skills.name: Shared skills and a marketplace
roadmap.teams.skills.text: Share an agent's skills by grant, promote them team-wide with approval, import them from Git, and find reviewed items in a public catalog.
roadmap.teams.memory.name: Memory for people and rooms
roadmap.teams.memory.text: Keep what an agent has learned for each person and each shared room, apart from the others.
roadmap.teams.more: Also: admin controls for models, sharing and strictness · a self-hosted team server · sign-in for teams (SSO and MFA) · usage limits per person, token or agent · read-only reports to share without sharing terminals · a phone view of the “For you” list · reviewed connectors to company tools · more chat apps · small internal web apps published to chosen people.
roadmap.cloud.title: Cloud
roadmap.cloud.sub: Agents that do not need your laptop awake.
roadmap.cloud.sandbox.name: Sandboxed agents in the cloud
roadmap.cloud.sandbox.text: Run an agent in an isolated cloud sandbox and watch it on the same canvas as your local ones. Sandboxes sleep when idle, wake on demand and keep storage between runs.
roadmap.cloud.pool.name: A pool of agents
roadmap.cloud.pool.text: Describe the work and let a pool of agents pick it up, instead of naming a terminal for each task.
roadmap.cloud.envs.name: Ready-made environments
roadmap.cloud.envs.text: Save dependencies, tools, skills, files and variables once, and start any new terminal or cloud agent from them.
roadmap.cloud.long.name: Long, multi-phase work
roadmap.cloud.long.text: Tasks that run for hours or days in stages, with a check-in after each stage and progress that survives restarts.
roadmap.cloud.deploy.name: One-command cloud deploy
roadmap.cloud.deploy.text: Put a team's shared Aubergine on your own cloud account with one command.
roadmap.cloud.see.name: Work you can see
roadmap.cloud.see.text: A cloud agent hands back screenshots or a short recording of what it built, in your “For you” list.
roadmap.cloud.more: Also: MCP over HTTP, for agents on other machines · tested Linux support · shell integration beyond zsh.
roadmap.control.title: Control
roadmap.control.sub: How much an agent may do, and a record of what it did.
roadmap.control.approval.name: Approval modes
roadmap.control.approval.text: Choose how much an agent may do alone: approve every action, approve the risky ones, or none.
roadmap.control.policy.name: Command policy and screening
roadmap.control.policy.text: Rules for commands that need approval or are always refused, and optional screening of outside content before an agent reads it.
roadmap.control.risk.name: Risk levels per repository
roadmap.control.risk.text: Stricter limits where it matters, looser where it does not.
roadmap.control.audit.name: A full audit trail
roadmap.control.audit.text: A record of who or what did what, per project, beyond the token calls recorded today.
roadmap.control.undo.name: Undo an agent's work
roadmap.control.undo.text: Roll a working copy back to before a task, or discard its branch in one step.
roadmap.control.admin.name: Admin controls
roadmap.control.admin.text: Team-wide settings for which models may be used and how sharing works.
roadmap.control.more: Also: model choice per terminal, task or schedule.

roadmap.quality.sub: Checks that happen before work is called done.
roadmap.quality.gates.name: Quality gates
roadmap.quality.gates.text: A run cannot finish until review, tests or a security check report a pass.
roadmap.quality.review.name: Pull request review
roadmap.quality.review.text: An agent reviews a pull request and reports to your “For you” list.
roadmap.quality.browser.name: Browser-driven testing
roadmap.quality.browser.text: An agent drives a browser to test a change and hands back the results.
roadmap.quality.plan.name: Plan before build
roadmap.quality.plan.text: An agent proposes a plan and waits for your approval before touching files.
roadmap.quality.recipes.name: Task recipes
roadmap.quality.recipes.text: Ready-made workflows for test generation, review, dependency and secret scans, and keeping docs current.
roadmap.quality.metrics.name: Outcome metrics
roadmap.quality.metrics.text: Time from task to done, how often an agent waited on you, and usage by who started it, per project.

roadmap.everywhere.sdk.text: The typed client as an installable package, then clients for other languages such as Python.

roadmap.everywhere.editor.text: Show your terminals and “For you” list inside VS Code and similar editors, without leaving the editor.

roadmap.everywhere.desktop.text: A packaged app with a menu-bar icon, instead of a browser tab.

faq.meta.title: Aubergine FAQ: agents, privacy and requirements
faq.meta.description: Answers about Aubergine: what it is, what it needs, whether it is private, how it works with coding agents, and what is planned.
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.lead: Short answers. The guides go deeper.
faq.what.a: A local, browser-based canvas of terminal sessions. Each terminal is a node you can arrange and use, so you can run several coding agents at once and see which one is waiting for you.
faq.free.q: Is Aubergine free and open source?
faq.free.a: Yes. It is free and its source is on GitHub.
faq.need.q: What do I need to run Aubergine?
faq.need.a: macOS with tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer; the installer also needs pnpm. On Linux it has been run in containers only. On Windows it runs only inside WSL 2, which has not been tried yet: see the guide for Windows.
faq.agents.q: Does it work with any coding agent?
faq.agents.a: Aubergine runs ordinary terminals, so any command-line agent can run in one. What Aubergine does by itself for an agent, such as seeing that it waits, is built for Claude Code; any other agent, Codex among them, can report its status through the aubergine commands and a local API, and can use an MCP server that lists only what its token allows.
faq.send.q: Does Aubergine send my terminals or code anywhere?
faq.send.a: No. Everything runs on your own computer. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only.
faq.model.q: Does Aubergine call an AI model?
faq.model.a: No. Your agents do. Aubergine only runs their terminals and keeps track of them, and holds no key for any model.
faq.close.q: What happens to my terminals when I close the browser?
faq.close.a: They keep running. Each session is a tmux session that outlives both the browser and the Aubergine server.
faq.waiting.q: How do I know which agent is waiting for me?
faq.waiting.a: Each terminal shows whether it is busy, idle or waiting. The count beside For you at the top of the page and the For you list gather everything that needs you.
faq.apart.q: How do I keep two agents from editing the same files?
faq.apart.a: Start each terminal in its own working copy: its own checkout on its own branch. Aubergine never merges or pushes for you.
faq.steps.q: Can I give an agent a list of steps to follow?
faq.steps.a: Yes. A workflow is an ordered list of steps, with a strip that shows where the agent is. A step can wait for you to approve or send back.
faq.talk.q: Can agents talk to each other?
faq.talk.a: Yes, within limits. Messages between terminals have named senders, pauses and blocks, and are closed by default for each canvas.
faq.api.a: Yes. A local HTTP API with scoped tokens, a typed client, and an MCP server that lists only the tools a credential may use.
faq.focus.q: Can I open one terminal by itself?
faq.focus.a: Yes. Tab ↗ in a terminal's title opens it in a browser tab of its own, the same terminal and not a copy, with its details and note beside it when you ask. Closing the tab ends nothing.
faq.fields.q: Can I keep a ticket or an owner with a terminal?
faq.fields.a: Yes. A terminal has fields, pairs of a label and a value, in its details. The agent in it can set its own with aubergine field set; where you set the same label, yours stays.
faq.cloud.q: Will Aubergine support several people or agents in the cloud?
faq.cloud.a: Both are planned and neither is built. See the roadmap. Today everything runs on one computer.
faq.installer.q: What does the installer change on my computer?
faq.installer.a: Two things: the install folder (~/.aubergine) and one link named aubergine. It never uses sudo, never edits your shell startup files and never installs Node.js, pnpm or tmux.

compare.meta.title: 7 tools for running coding agents, compared | Aubergine
compare.meta.description: Aubergine beside Conductor, Claude Squad, Vibe Kanban, cmux, Warp and Paradev: what each is, where it runs, what it costs and what closing it ends.
compare.title: Tools for running several coding agents, compared
compare.lead: Seven tools for the same moment: more than one coding agent at work, and you in the middle. Here is Aubergine beside Conductor, Claude Squad, Vibe Kanban, cmux, Warp and Paradev, with a page for each.
compare.how: How this was written. What these pages say about another tool is from that tool's own site, documentation and repository as read on 26 November 2026, and each page links to them. We have not run the other tools. Where their documentation says nothing, the page says that nothing was found, not that the tool cannot do it. These tools change fast: if something here is wrong or out of date, tell us and it will be corrected.
compare.table.title: All seven, side by side
compare.each.title: One page for each
compare.each.text: Each page has the whole table for the two, where they differ, and what the other tool has that Aubergine does not.
compare.around.title: What Aubergine is built around
compare.around.terminals: Ordinary terminals. An agent runs in Aubergine as it runs in any terminal app. There is no chat view over it and nothing between you and what it prints.
compare.around.canvas: All of them in sight. Terminals stand side by side on a canvas you pan and zoom, with one list of every terminal and its state in words. See Find the right terminal.
compare.around.tmux: Closing the window ends nothing. Every terminal is a tmux session, so the browser and Aubergine itself can stop while your agents go on. See what a restart keeps.
compare.around.local: Your computer only. No account, no cloud, no paid plan and no model of its own; the server listens on 127.0.0.1. See security.
compare.around.decide: A person decides. What an agent proposes waits for your review, an approval in a workflow is yours alone, and one list, For you, holds everything that waits on you. See the queue.
compare.it.title: If your IT department has to approve it
compare.it.text: Some companies do not allow developer tools that need an account with their maker, that send code or terminal output to the maker's cloud, or whose source cannot be read. Aubergine has none of these: it runs on your own computer, its server listens on 127.0.0.1, it has no account and no cloud, it calls no model, and it is open source under the MIT license, so a security team can read all of it.
compare.it.agents: The agents you run in it are a separate question. Each sends what it sends to its own provider and needs its own approval; Aubergine changes nothing about that. What Aubergine protects, and what it does not, is on the security page.
compare.lacks.title: What Aubergine does not have
compare.lacks.app: No desktop app and no phone app. It is a page in your browser. Another device can be paired through a proxy you run; that was run once on one Mac and never on a real phone.
compare.lacks.merge: No pull requests and no merging. It shows what changed in a working copy, file by file, and never commits, pushes, rebases or merges.
compare.lacks.cloud: No cloud. Agents run on the computer Aubergine runs on, and schedules fire only while it is on.
compare.lacks.sound: No sound and no push. Notifications come from an Aubergine page open in your browser.
compare.lacks.platforms: Built for macOS. On Linux it has been run in containers only; on Windows it runs only inside WSL 2, which has not been tried.
compare.lacks.agents: Most for Claude Code. Any command-line agent runs in a terminal, but what Aubergine does by itself for an agent (seeing that it waits, resuming a conversation) is built for Claude Code; another agent reports through the aubergine commands.
compare.q.best.q: What is the best tool for running several Claude Code agents at once?
compare.q.best.a: It depends on what you want around the agents. For a Mac app with diffs, pull requests and merging: Conductor or Paradev. For a program inside the terminal you already use: Claude Squad. For a board of issues: Vibe Kanban. For a native Mac terminal: cmux. For a terminal with its own agent and cloud agents: Warp. For plain terminals side by side in a browser page, kept running by tmux, with no account: Aubergine.
compare.q.open.q: Which of these tools are open source?
compare.q.open.a: As read on 26 November 2026: Aubergine (MIT), Paradev (MIT), Vibe Kanban (Apache-2.0), Claude Squad (AGPL-3.0), the cmux app (GPL-3.0-or-later) and the Warp client (AGPL-3.0). Conductor's terms call it proprietary.
compare.q.linux.q: Which of these tools run on Linux or Windows?
compare.q.linux.a: By their own documentation: Warp on macOS, Windows and Linux; Vibe Kanban on all three; Claude Squad on macOS and Linux, and on Windows with tmux through WSL; Paradev on macOS with an experimental Linux build; Conductor and cmux on macOS only. Aubergine is built for macOS, has been run on Linux in containers only, and runs on Windows only inside WSL 2, not yet tried.
compare.q.close.q: Which keep agents running after you close the app?
compare.q.close.a: Aubergine and Claude Squad run each agent in a tmux session. Paradev documents a background daemon that keeps terminals when its window closes. cmux keeps live processes only in its opt-in tmux mode. Conductor says local sessions end with the app. Warp restores windows and recent output, not running programs. Each of Conductor, cmux, Warp and Paradev also has a cloud where agents go on. None, Aubergine included, keeps a local agent running through a restart of the computer.
compare.row.waits: When an agent waits or is done
compare.a.form: A server on your own computer and a page in your browser
compare.a.runs: macOS; Linux in containers only; Windows inside WSL 2, not tried. Needs tmux and Node.js
compare.a.price: MIT, free; no paid plan and no account
compare.a.agents: Any command-line agent; more by itself for Claude Code
compare.a.layout: Terminals side by side on a canvas, and one list of them all
compare.a.apart: A Git worktree on its own branch for a terminal, when you ask for one
compare.a.closed: Terminals go on in tmux; a restart of the computer ends what ran
compare.a.waits: The terminal's color, a count at the top, a key to the next one, notifications from the open page; no sound
compare.a.review: What changed, file by file; no commit, push, pull request or merge
compare.a.device: A browser you pair, through a proxy you run; no app; not tried on a real phone
compare.a.programs: An HTTP API with scoped tokens, the aubergine command, an MCP server
compare.a.timed: A queue with a limit, schedules by time of day, workflows with approvals
vs.conductor.name: Conductor
vs.conductor.meta.title: Aubergine vs Conductor: a free, open-source alternative
vs.conductor.meta.description: Both run coding agents in parallel in Git worktrees. Conductor is a Mac app with a cloud; Aubergine is open source and keeps terminals running in tmux.
vs.conductor.title: Aubergine vs Conductor
vs.conductor.lead: Both run several coding agents at once, each in its own Git worktree. Conductor is a Mac app with chats, a diff viewer and a cloud. Aubergine is a free, open-source server on your own computer that shows ordinary terminals side by side in a browser page.
vs.conductor.how: Where this comes from. What is said here about Conductor is from its documentation and its changelog as read on 26 November 2026. We have not run Conductor. If something is wrong or out of date, tell us.
vs.conductor.status: Where Conductor stands. On 4 November 2026 its changelog said Conductor was joining Meta and would wind down; on 13 November it said Conductor is not shutting down. Parts of its site still carried the first message when this was written. Read its changelog for where it stands now.
vs.conductor.is.title: What Conductor is
vs.conductor.is.text: By its own description, a Mac app that runs many coding agents in parallel on your codebase. Each piece of work is a workspace: a Git worktree on one branch, with chat, terminal and browser tabs. It runs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode with the sign-ins already on your Mac, and has a diff viewer, pull requests, an iOS app and a paid cloud where agents run in sandboxes.
vs.conductor.pick.title: Which to pick
vs.conductor.pick.them: Pick Conductor if you want a Mac app that takes a task from a prompt to a merged pull request, with a cloud for work that goes on while your Mac is off.
vs.conductor.pick.us: Pick Aubergine if you want your agents as plain terminals you can see all at once, going on in tmux when the window closes, with nothing to sign in to and the source open.
vs.conductor.differs.title: Where they differ
vs.conductor.d1: Terminals, not chats. Conductor shows an agent as a chat in a workspace, with a terminal mode beside it. Aubergine shows the agent's own terminal, as it runs in any terminal app, and lays many of them out on a canvas you pan and zoom.
vs.conductor.d2: What closing it ends. Conductor's documentation says local sessions end when you close the app or shut down the Mac, and that cloud sessions go on. In Aubergine every terminal is a tmux session: closing the browser or stopping Aubergine ends nothing. A restart of the computer does, in both.
vs.conductor.d3: Nothing outside your computer. Conductor documents an account, a cloud, a relay for its phone app and usage analytics. Aubergine has no account and no service of its own: the server listens on 127.0.0.1, and use from another device goes through a proxy you run.
vs.conductor.has.title: What Conductor has that Aubergine does not
vs.conductor.h1: A diff viewer where you comment on lines and send the comments back to the agent, then pull requests, checks and merging. Aubergine shows what changed in a working copy and never commits, pushes or merges.
vs.conductor.h2: A cloud where agents go on with your Mac off, and routines that run there on a schedule. Aubergine's schedules fire on your computer, while it is on.
vs.conductor.h3: An iOS app and completion sounds. Aubergine has no app and plays no sound.
vs.conductor.q1.q: Is Aubergine an alternative to Conductor?
vs.conductor.q1.a: For running several command-line agents on your own computer, yes: each agent has a terminal on a canvas and, when you ask, its own Git worktree. It is not a like-for-like replacement: Aubergine has no chat view, no pull requests or merging, no cloud and no phone app.
vs.conductor.q2.a: No: its terms call it proprietary, and we found no public repository. Its documentation says the local app is free to use and that cloud workspaces need a paid plan. Aubergine is under the MIT license and has no paid plan.
vs.conductor.q3.q: Does Conductor run on Linux or Windows?
vs.conductor.q3.a: Its documentation says it is not available for Windows or Linux yet. Aubergine is built for macOS, has been run on Linux in containers only, and on Windows runs only inside WSL 2, which has not been tried.
vs.conductor.q4.q: Can I use Conductor and Aubergine together?
vs.conductor.q4.a: Nothing stops it: both work in Git worktrees of the same repository, each making its own. We have not run the two side by side.
vs.conductor.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with Conductor or its makers. Conductor is the name of their product: its terms name Melty Labs, Inc., and its site says Conductor from Meta.

vs.claude-squad.name: Claude Squad
vs.claude-squad.meta.title: Aubergine vs Claude Squad: tmux and worktrees, two ways
vs.claude-squad.meta.description: Both run each coding agent in a tmux session and a Git worktree. Claude Squad is a program in your terminal; Aubergine is a canvas in your browser.
vs.claude-squad.title: Aubergine vs Claude Squad
vs.claude-squad.lead: The two stand on the same ground: each agent in a tmux session, each in its own Git worktree, both free and open source. Claude Squad is a program inside your terminal. Aubergine is a page in your browser where the terminals stand side by side.
vs.claude-squad.how: Where this comes from. What is said here about Claude Squad is from its repository and README as read on 26 November 2026. We have not run Claude Squad. If something is wrong or out of date, tell us.
vs.claude-squad.is.title: What Claude Squad is
vs.claude-squad.is.text: By its own description, a terminal app that manages several Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and other local agents in separate workspaces. You start it as cs: a list of sessions with a preview and a diff tab, in one terminal window. Each session is a tmux session in a Git worktree on its own branch. It needs tmux and gh, and is under the AGPL-3.0 license.
vs.claude-squad.pick.title: Which to pick
vs.claude-squad.pick.them: Pick Claude Squad if you live in a terminal and want one small program there that starts agents in worktrees and pushes their branches, and nothing more.
vs.claude-squad.pick.us: Pick Aubergine if you want to see several agents working at once, know which one waits for you, and have a queue, schedules and an API around them.
vs.claude-squad.differs.title: Where they differ
vs.claude-squad.d1: One at a time, or all at once. Claude Squad shows a list and a preview of the session you chose. Aubergine draws every terminal live on a canvas, so five agents are five terminals in sight, and one list says the state of each in words.
vs.claude-squad.d2: Who waits. We found nothing in Claude Squad's README about being told that an agent waits or is done. Aubergine marks a waiting terminal in color, counts what waits at the top, goes to the next one with a key, and can send a notification from the open page.
vs.claude-squad.d3: What is around the agents. Aubergine has a queue of tasks with a limit, schedules, workflows with steps a person approves, notes and fields on each terminal, an HTTP API and an MCP server. Claude Squad keeps to sessions and their branches.
vs.claude-squad.has.title: What Claude Squad has that Aubergine does not
vs.claude-squad.h1: It runs inside the terminal you already have open, with no server and no browser. It works over SSH like any terminal program; Aubergine from elsewhere needs a tunnel or a proxy.
vs.claude-squad.h2: It commits and pushes a branch for you, and pauses a session by committing its work. Aubergine never commits or pushes.
vs.claude-squad.h3: An experimental mode that accepts an agent's prompts by itself. Aubergine never answers an agent for you.
vs.claude-squad.q1.q: Is Aubergine an alternative to Claude Squad?
vs.claude-squad.q1.a: Yes, for the same job done another way. Both run each agent in a tmux session and can give each a Git worktree on its own branch. Claude Squad does it from a program in your terminal; Aubergine from a page in your browser with every terminal in sight.
vs.claude-squad.q2.a: Yes. Claude Squad lists tmux as a prerequisite and makes a tmux session for each agent. Aubergine needs tmux 3.2 or newer and runs it on a socket of its own with its own configuration, so your own tmux is left alone.
vs.claude-squad.q3.q: Does Claude Squad work with agents other than Claude Code?
vs.claude-squad.q3.a: Its README says the default program is claude and that another, such as Codex, Gemini or Aider, is named with -p. Aubergine runs any command-line program in a terminal; what it does by itself for an agent is built for Claude Code.
vs.claude-squad.q4.a: Claude Squad is under the AGPL-3.0, Aubergine under the MIT license. Both are free.
vs.claude-squad.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with Claude Squad or with Anthropic. Claude Squad is the name of the smtg-ai project; Claude is a trademark of Anthropic.

vs.vibe-kanban.name: Vibe Kanban
vs.vibe-kanban.meta.title: Aubergine vs Vibe Kanban: an open-source alternative
vs.vibe-kanban.meta.description: Both are local, open source and shown in your browser. Vibe Kanban plans work as issues on a board; Aubergine shows the agents as terminals side by side.
vs.vibe-kanban.title: Aubergine vs Vibe Kanban
vs.vibe-kanban.lead: Both are open source, run on your own computer and are used in a browser. Vibe Kanban starts from the work: issues on a board, each handed to an agent. Aubergine starts from the agents: terminals side by side, with a queue beside them.
vs.vibe-kanban.how: Where this comes from. What is said here about Vibe Kanban is from its documentation and its repository as read on 26 November 2026. We have not run Vibe Kanban. If something is wrong or out of date, tell us.
vs.vibe-kanban.status: Where Vibe Kanban stands. On 10 April 2026 its makers wrote that bloop, the company behind it, was shutting down, that the project goes on as open source maintained by its community, and that its remote services would be removed while local workspaces keep working. Its documentation and pricing page still described those services when this was written; releases have continued.
vs.vibe-kanban.is.title: What Vibe Kanban is
vs.vibe-kanban.is.text: By its own description, a kanban board for developers to track coding tasks with coding agents. npx vibe-kanban starts a local server and opens its page. An issue becomes a workspace: Git worktrees for the repositories you chose, a conversation with one of ten or more agents it knows by name, the changes beside it, then a pull request and a merge. It is under the Apache-2.0 license.
vs.vibe-kanban.pick.title: Which to pick
vs.vibe-kanban.pick.them: Pick Vibe Kanban if you think in issues: plan on a board, hand each card to an agent, review its diff with comments, and merge.
vs.vibe-kanban.pick.us: Pick Aubergine if you want the agents themselves in view as terminals that outlive the window, and work handed out from a queue only when you say so.
vs.vibe-kanban.differs.title: Where they differ
vs.vibe-kanban.d1: A conversation or a terminal. Vibe Kanban shows an agent as a conversation panel with its changes beside it. Aubergine shows the agent's own terminal, and many of them at once on a canvas.
vs.vibe-kanban.d2: Any program. Vibe Kanban lists the agents it supports by name. An Aubergine terminal is a shell: any command-line agent runs in it, and so does a build, a test run or a server. What Aubergine does by itself for an agent is built for Claude Code.
vs.vibe-kanban.d3: What closing it ends. We found nothing in Vibe Kanban's documentation about what happens to a running agent when its server stops. In Aubergine every terminal is a tmux session, and stopping Aubergine or closing the browser ends nothing.
vs.vibe-kanban.has.title: What Vibe Kanban has that Aubergine does not
vs.vibe-kanban.h1: A kanban board of issues with priorities, tags and sub-issues. Aubergine has a queue of tasks and a board of running workflows, not an issue tracker.
vs.vibe-kanban.h2: Diffs with inline comments sent back to the agent, then pull requests, rebase and merge. Aubergine shows what changed and never commits or merges.
vs.vibe-kanban.h3: Windows among its documented platforms, sounds, and a longer list of agents it knows by name.
vs.vibe-kanban.q1.q: Is Aubergine an alternative to Vibe Kanban?
vs.vibe-kanban.q1.a: For running several agents locally in Git worktrees and seeing which needs you, yes. It is a different shape: Aubergine has terminals on a canvas and a queue of tasks where Vibe Kanban has a board of issues with conversations, and Aubergine opens no pull request and merges nothing.
vs.vibe-kanban.q2.a: Its makers wrote on 10 April 2026 that the company behind it was shutting down and that the project continues as open source maintained by its community. Its repository has had releases since. Read its repository for where it stands now.
vs.vibe-kanban.q3.a: Yes. Each is a server on your own computer with a page in your browser. Vibe Kanban documents an optional sign-in for its board and team features; Aubergine has no account at all.
vs.vibe-kanban.q4.a: Vibe Kanban names more than ten, among them Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Amp, Cursor and OpenCode. Aubergine runs any command-line program in a terminal; starting an agent from the menu, seeing that it waits and resuming its conversation are built for Claude Code.
vs.vibe-kanban.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with Vibe Kanban or its makers. Vibe Kanban is the name of the project begun by Bloop AI Limited.

vs.cmux.name: cmux
vs.cmux.meta.title: Aubergine vs cmux: two terminals built for coding agents
vs.cmux.meta.description: Both run any command-line agent in a real terminal and show which one needs you. cmux is a native macOS app; Aubergine is a canvas in your browser.
vs.cmux.title: Aubergine vs cmux
vs.cmux.lead: The closest pair on these pages: both are terminals made for coding agents, both run any agent you can start from a command line, both are open source. cmux is a native macOS terminal app. Aubergine is a server on your computer and a canvas of terminals in your browser.
vs.cmux.how: Where this comes from. What is said here about cmux is from its site and documentation and its repository as read on 26 November 2026. We have not run cmux. If something is wrong or out of date, tell us.
vs.cmux.is.title: What cmux is
vs.cmux.is.text: By its own description, a macOS terminal built on libghostty with vertical tabs and notifications for coding agents, written in Swift. A sidebar lists workspaces with their branch, pull request, folder and latest notification; a workspace splits into panes with tabs. Every action is also a command and a message on a Unix socket. The app is under the GPL-3.0-or-later license and free; cloud machines and an iOS app in beta come with an account and paid plans.
vs.cmux.pick.title: Which to pick
vs.cmux.pick.them: Pick cmux if you want a fast native Mac terminal app with panes, an in-app browser and macOS notifications, and you script your own way of working on top of it.
vs.cmux.pick.us: Pick Aubergine if you want agents that go on when the app is closed without choosing a mode, a worktree per agent made for you, and a queue, schedules and approvals already built.
vs.cmux.differs.title: Where they differ
vs.cmux.d1: What closing it ends. cmux documents that quitting saves the layout and folders and that live processes are not kept, unless you opt in to its local tmux mode. In Aubergine tmux is not a mode: every terminal is a tmux session from the start. Neither keeps a process through a restart of the computer.
vs.cmux.d2: A primitive, or the things around it. cmux calls itself a primitive, not a solution, and gives you a command and a socket to build with. Aubergine comes with working copies in Git worktrees, a queue with a limit, schedules, workflows with approvals and one list of what waits for you.
vs.cmux.d3: An app or a page. cmux is a Mac app drawn by the system. Aubergine is a page in a browser: slower to draw than a native terminal, and reachable from another browser you pair through a proxy you run.
vs.cmux.has.title: What cmux has that Aubergine does not
vs.cmux.h1: A native terminal on libghostty, split panes, and an in-app browser its command can drive. Aubergine draws terminals in a browser page and has no panes: terminals are placed on a canvas.
vs.cmux.h2: macOS notifications and a custom command when a pane needs you, set off by the escape sequences terminals already use, for any program. Aubergine sees an agent wait through hooks built for Claude Code, and notifies from the open page only.
vs.cmux.h3: cmux ssh for a workspace on a remote machine, an iOS app in beta, and cloud machines on its paid plans.
vs.cmux.q1.q: Is Aubergine an alternative to cmux?
vs.cmux.q1.a: Yes: both are terminals for running several coding agents and seeing which one needs you. cmux is a native macOS app; Aubergine runs in a browser on top of tmux, and adds working copies, a queue, schedules and workflows.
vs.cmux.q2.a: No. Its documentation says tmux is not required, and offers an opt-in local tmux mode for keeping live processes when cmux quits. Aubergine needs tmux 3.2 or newer and runs every terminal in it.
vs.cmux.q3.q: Does cmux run on Linux or Windows?
vs.cmux.q3.a: Its README says macOS only, for now, on macOS 14 or later. Aubergine is built for macOS, has been run on Linux in containers only, and on Windows runs only inside WSL 2, which has not been tried.
vs.cmux.q4.q: Are both free and open source?
vs.cmux.q4.a: The cmux app is under the GPL-3.0-or-later license and free, with paid plans for its cloud; its server software has a different license. Aubergine is under the MIT license and has no paid plan.
vs.cmux.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with cmux or its makers. cmux is the name of a product of Manaflow, Inc.
vs.cmux.c.price: GPL-3.0-or-later app, free, no account needed; paid plans for its cloud

vs.warp.name: Warp
vs.warp.meta.title: Aubergine vs Warp for running several coding agents
vs.warp.meta.description: Warp is a desktop terminal with its own agent, paid plans and a cloud. Aubergine calls no model: it runs the agents you already use, side by side.
vs.warp.title: Aubergine vs Warp
vs.warp.lead: Warp is a whole terminal app, with an agent of its own, plans and a cloud, that also runs other command-line agents in tabs and panes. Aubergine is narrower: it calls no model and replaces no terminal app. It runs the agents you already use side by side in a browser page, and keeps them running.
vs.warp.how: Where this comes from. What is said here about Warp is from its documentation and its pricing page as read on 26 November 2026, and only about running several coding agents; Warp does much else. We have not run Warp for this. If something is wrong or out of date, tell us.
vs.warp.is.title: What Warp is
vs.warp.is.text: By its own description, an agentic development environment: a desktop terminal for macOS, Windows and Linux whose client is open source under the AGPL-3.0. It has its own Warp Agent, which calls models through Warp or with your own keys, and it runs other command-line agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI in tabs and panes, with a panel of all active agents, notifications, a code review panel, and cloud agents that run on a schedule.
vs.warp.pick.title: Which to pick
vs.warp.pick.them: Pick Warp if you want one terminal app for everything, on Windows and Linux too, with its own agent built in and cloud agents you can schedule.
vs.warp.pick.us: Pick Aubergine if you already have a terminal and agents you like, and want only what is missing between them: all of them in sight, kept running, with no account and no model of its own.
vs.warp.differs.title: Where they differ
vs.warp.d1: A model of its own, or none. Warp has its own agent, with plans that pay for its use and an option to bring your own keys. Aubergine calls no model and holds no key: the agents in its terminals are the ones you installed and signed in to yourself.
vs.warp.d2: What closing it ends. Warp documents that it restores windows, tabs, panes and recent output; we found nothing saying a running program is kept. In Aubergine every terminal is a tmux session, so an agent goes on when the browser or Aubergine itself stops.
vs.warp.d3: Where your agents can be reached from. Warp publishes a running session to its cloud so you can steer it from a phone or a browser. Aubergine has no cloud: another device is a browser you pair with a code, through a proxy you run on your own machine, tried once on one Mac.
vs.warp.has.title: What Warp has that Aubergine does not
vs.warp.h1: Windows and Linux as documented platforms, as a desktop app. Aubergine is built for macOS.
vs.warp.h2: An agent of its own, and cloud agents that start on a schedule or from another service such as Slack, Linear or GitHub. Aubergine starts nothing from outside and reaches no network for a schedule.
vs.warp.h3: Everything else a terminal app is: its editor for commands, blocks of output, and notifications for more than one agent. Aubergine sees an agent wait through hooks built for Claude Code.
vs.warp.q1.q: Is Aubergine an alternative to Warp?
vs.warp.q1.a: Only for one thing Warp does: running several command-line coding agents and seeing which needs you. Aubergine is not a terminal app and has no agent of its own. You can keep Warp, or any terminal, and use Aubergine for the agents.
vs.warp.q2.q: Do I need an account or a paid plan?
vs.warp.q2.a: Warp's documentation says logging in is optional for the terminal, and its pricing page lists a free plan and paid ones. Aubergine has no account and no plans.
vs.warp.q3.a: Its documentation says Warp's client is open source under the AGPL-3.0. Aubergine is under the MIT license.
vs.warp.q4.q: Can I use Warp and Aubergine together?
vs.warp.q4.a: Yes, as with any terminal app. Aubergine's terminals are tmux sessions, and aubergine attach <name> shows one in a window of the terminal app you run it from. We have not tried that in Warp.
vs.warp.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with Warp. Warp is a trademark of Denver Technologies, Inc., which does business as Warp.

vs.paradev.name: Paradev
vs.paradev.meta.title: Aubergine vs Paradev (formerly Superset): an alternative
vs.paradev.meta.description: Paradev, once called Superset, and Aubergine are both MIT-licensed and work in Git worktrees. Paradev is a desktop app with paid plans; Aubergine is free.
vs.paradev.title: Aubergine vs Paradev, formerly Superset
vs.paradev.lead: Paradev is the desktop app that was called Superset until October 2026. Like Aubergine it is under the MIT license, runs any command-line agent and works in Git worktrees. It is an app with plans, phone apps and a cloud; Aubergine is a server on your own computer and a page in your browser, with none of those.
vs.paradev.how: Where this comes from. What is said here about Paradev is from its documentation, its changelog and its repository as read on 26 November 2026. We have not run Paradev. If something is wrong or out of date, tell us.
vs.paradev.status: The name. Its changelog for 25 October 2026 says Superset is now Paradev and that accounts, workspaces, settings and the superset command carry over. It is not Apache Superset, the data tool.
vs.paradev.is.title: What Paradev is
vs.paradev.is.text: By its own description, the open-source workspace for Claude Code, Codex and any coding agent: a desktop app, not a terminal app, in which agents run as a chat or in a terminal. Every task has its own worktree, branch and terminal; one sidebar shows every session by project. It has a diff viewer with pull request checks and merging, a command, an SDK and an MCP server, and on paid plans phone apps, remote access, cloud workspaces and automations.
vs.paradev.pick.title: Which to pick
vs.paradev.pick.them: Pick Paradev if you want a desktop app that makes a worktree for every task and takes it through diff, checks and merge, with phone apps and a cloud when you pay for them.
vs.paradev.pick.us: Pick Aubergine if you want every part free on your own computer with no account: terminals side by side, a queue, schedules and use from another device.
vs.paradev.differs.title: Where they differ
vs.paradev.d1: What is free. Paradev lists a free plan for one person with local workspaces, the app and the command; automations, phone apps and remote access are on paid plans. Aubergine has no plans: its queue, its schedules and use from another device are all in the one MIT-licensed program, with no account.
vs.paradev.d2: A sidebar or a canvas. Paradev shows sessions in a sidebar with tabs and panes. Aubergine places terminals on a canvas you pan and zoom, so many are live in sight at once, with one list of them all beside it.
vs.paradev.d3: How terminals outlive the window. Both keep agents running when the window closes: Paradev through its own background daemon, which its documentation says ends every terminal when you quit Paradev completely; Aubergine through tmux, which goes on when Aubergine itself is stopped. A restart of the computer ends them in both.
vs.paradev.has.title: What Paradev has that Aubergine does not
vs.paradev.h1: A diff viewer in which you comment on and edit an agent's changes, watch a pull request's checks and merge. Aubergine shows what changed and never commits, pushes or merges.
vs.paradev.h2: A desktop app, iOS and Android apps, cloud workspaces, and a chime and a dock badge when an agent needs you. Aubergine is a browser page and plays no sound.
vs.paradev.h3: Automations set off by a review request, a Slack message, an issue or a webhook, and hooks it installs so that many agents report their state. Aubergine starts nothing from outside, and sees an agent wait by itself only for Claude Code.
vs.paradev.q1.q: Is Aubergine an alternative to Paradev (Superset)?
vs.paradev.q1.a: For running several command-line agents locally, each in its own Git worktree, yes, and with every feature free. It is not a like-for-like replacement: Aubergine has no desktop or phone app, no diff comments, no pull requests or merging and no cloud.
vs.paradev.q2.q: Is Superset the same as Paradev?
vs.paradev.q2.a: Yes. Its changelog for 25 October 2026 says Superset is now Paradev, and its README says the command is still superset. Neither is related to Apache Superset.
vs.paradev.q3.a: Both are under the MIT license. Paradev also sells plans for its phone apps, remote access, cloud and automations; Aubergine sells nothing.
vs.paradev.q4.q: Does Paradev run on Linux or Windows?
vs.paradev.q4.a: Its documentation says macOS, with an experimental Linux build, and that Windows is not yet available. Aubergine is built for macOS, has been run on Linux in containers only, and on Windows runs only inside WSL 2, which has not been tried.
vs.paradev.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with Paradev or its makers, Superset Inc. Paradev and Superset are their names; neither they nor Aubergine are related to Apache Superset.

custom.meta.description: Ten color themes, a theme for each terminal, colors set by hand, fonts, cursor and keys, and how VS Code, kitty, tmux and others let you customize.
custom.title: Customize terminal themes, colors, fonts and keys
custom.lead: Choose the page's colors from ten themes, give each terminal a theme of its own, and set single colors, the terminal's font and cursor and every key, in Settings or in one settings file that describes itself.
custom.page.title: Ten color themes, light and dark
custom.page.text: Settings → Appearance starts with three choices: Light, Dark and Match the system, which is where a new install starts and which follows the system when it changes. Under them you choose a theme of each kind: Light, High contrast light, Solarized light or Gruvbox light; Dark, High contrast dark, Solarized dark, Gruvbox dark, Nord or Dracula. Each is shown with a small picture of its colors.
custom.page.at: A change applies at once to the page and to every terminal, without a reload, and is kept in the settings file, so every browser you open Aubergine in agrees. The palette has the same as commands, such as Color theme: Nord.
custom.own.title: A different color theme for each terminal
custom.own.text: Theme… in a terminal's menu draws that terminal in any of the ten themes, whatever the page is drawn in. Only its body changes: its title, its note and its details stay as the page is. A terminal without a theme of its own follows Terminal theme in Settings, the default for terminals, and without that, the page.
custom.menu.alt: A terminal's Theme… menu open on the canvas: Same as the default, now as the page, Dark; then the four light themes and the six dark ones, with Dracula ticked.
custom.menu.caption: Theme… in a terminal's menu: the default, or any of the ten.
custom.own.where: The same choice is in the terminal's row menu in the list, in its details and in the palette. A terminal and a frame can also have a color of their own, one of thirteen or Your own… for any color, and so can a canvas's tab; a terminal's color is its row's in the list too.
custom.colors.title: Set single colors by hand
custom.colors.text: Beyond the themes, 35 colors of the page can be set in the settings file, config.json, under appearance.colors: a color's name and a value written #rrggbb. Written at the top, a color is over every theme; written under a theme's ID in brackets, such as "[nord]", it is over that theme alone, and wins.
custom.colors.names: The names are the page's color tokens, such as bg, text, accent and terminal-bg; docs/design.md lists them. A wrong entry is skipped, and the rest of the file still counts; Settings → Appearance says which was skipped. Colors you set are yours: nothing checks that what you wrote can be read.
custom.files.title: Themes of your own, as files
custom.files.text: A theme of your own is a JSON file in themes/ in the data folder: one of the ten as its base, of the same kind, with any of the 35 colors over it, and a terminal's own colors: its words, the cursor, what is selected, and the sixteen colors a program asks for. It is listed after the ten of its kind, marked yours, and can be chosen wherever they can: for the page, as the default for terminals, or for one terminal. Shadows and the focus ring stay the base's, and nothing in a file is run.
custom.files.cli: aubergine theme new harbor --from nord writes a file to start from, with every color of the theme it is from; aubergine theme check says what is wrong in one; Read themes again in Settings picks up a change. Whether your colors can be read is yours to judge: Settings only says when text may be hard to read. docs/themes.md has the format.
custom.when.title: A theme for a project, and for terminals by tag
custom.when.project: A project can draw the page in a theme of its own while you look at it, so that a glance says where you are. In Projects…, When light and When dark beside a project choose one theme of each kind; As the page leaves it to Settings. In every other project the page is as you chose it, and a reload on that project's address is drawn in its theme from the first paint.
custom.when.tag: By tag, under Terminal theme in Settings, gives the terminals with a tag a theme of their own: every terminal tagged prod in Dracula, for example, at once and whatever the page is drawn in. The first line whose tag a terminal has wins, and a terminal's own theme comes before all of them. In the settings file it is appearance.byTag:
custom.when.accent: Often a different accent is enough. aubergine theme new teal --from nord --accent "#2f9e8f" writes a theme file that changes only Nord's accent and the five colors that go with it, worked out so that they can still be read. Choose it for a project or a tag like any other theme.
custom.text.title: Fonts, cursor and keyboard shortcuts
custom.text.font: Terminal text in Settings → Appearance sets the size of a terminal's text, from 8 to 32 pixels, and its font, as a list of which the first font found is used. Cursor sets its shape, block, bar or underline, and whether it blinks.
custom.keys.text: Every key can be changed. Add shortcuts to the settings file: a command's name with a chord, a list of chords, or null for no key. shortcutsInAppWindow takes the same and applies only where Aubergine is installed as an app with a window of its own. Reload the page, and the shortcut sheet (?), the palette and the tooltips show the keys as you set them.
custom.keys.check: A key set twice, or one that cannot be read, is reported at the top of the shortcut sheet and by the server, and the rest of the file still applies. A plain key, or Ctrl or Option with a key, works only while no terminal has the keyboard, so that every program in a terminal still gets the keys it needs. More in Keyboard, in the README.
custom.tpl.title: Choose what a title and a row say
custom.tpl.text: After a terminal's name, its title and its row in the list say what two templates say: text with placeholders such as {state}, {folder}, {time} and {field:Ticket}. Change them in Settings → Appearance → Titles and rows, where the real title and row are drawn under each field as you type, or in the settings file. Here the title says the state, the folder, the field Ticket, the links and the tags, and the row the state, the step of a run, the branch and the time:
custom.tpl.rule: A placeholder with nothing to say is left out with the text that leads to it: on a terminal with no ticket, links or tags, that title says only its state and its folder, with no dot left over. A template holds text and placeholders only, no markup and no style; each is drawn as the page draws that thing elsewhere, the state in its color and a link as a chip. A wrong placeholder is said under the field and skipped, and Reset puts back exactly what is drawn without a template. Every placeholder is in docs/templates.md.
custom.css.title: Your own stylesheet
custom.css.text: For anything the settings do not reach, write a stylesheet of your own: custom.css in the data folder. The server links it as the last thing in the page's head, so it is there from the first paint, and a rule of yours wins over one of the app's that is as specific, without !important. aubergine css new writes one to start from, and Settings → Appearance → Your stylesheet says whether it is found, switches it off and reads it again without a reload.
custom.css.hooks: Rely on the hooks and on nothing else: every token (--accent, --radius-surface and the rest), the attributes on the page's root (data-theme, data-page), the parts marked data-part, and a terminal's own attributes (data-tags, data-state, data-name), the same on its node, its row and its browser tab of its own. They are listed in docs/hooks.md and kept from one release to the next; class names are not. Here the title of every terminal tagged prod is dark red, and the map is gone:
custom.css.tokens: And rounder corners everywhere, through two tokens:
custom.css.out: If a rule breaks the page, open it with ?plain after its address: it is sent without your stylesheet. Nothing a stylesheet names is fetched from another address: a picture, a font or a stylesheet comes from this server or from inline data, so a pasted snippet cannot send what is on your page elsewhere. That is a guard for a file you wrote or pasted, not a sandbox. It has been tried in Chromium only.
custom.file.title: One settings file that describes itself
custom.file.text: All of this is kept in config.json in Aubergine's data folder, and aubergine settings path prints where that is. Every key may be left out. A file that cannot be read means the defaults, never a server that will not start. Settings in the page writes only the keys it changes and leaves the rest of the file as you wrote it.
custom.file.schema: Each time it starts, the server writes config.schema.json beside the file. Add one line, and an editor that reads JSON Schema describes and completes every key:
custom.file.cli: aubergine settings list prints every key with its value now, marked where it is not the default, and aubergine settings schema prints the schema. docs/settings.md describes every key, its default, and whether Settings writes it or you do.
custom.file.all: In the page, Settings → Every setting lists the same keys with their values, and finds them as you type. A key that Settings changes takes you to its control; a key written by hand has Copy, for the line to add to the file. Nothing there changes a setting.
custom.all.alt: Settings, Every setting, opened, with “appearance” typed in its search: six keys, each with its value now, what it is and its default; five say Changed above, and appearance.colors has a Copy button.
custom.all.caption: Every setting, searched: what each key is, its value now and its default.
custom.file.browser: Some choices belong to this browser and are kept there: whether the canvases are tabs, one list or a column; where the bar over the canvas stands and whether it stays open; whether the side panel and the map are folded; the widths of the panel and of a terminal's details; and how the list of terminals is filtered, grouped and sorted.
custom.program.title: What a program or an agent may change, and what stays yours
custom.program.text: Through the local API, a program with an API token may arrange canvases with canvases:write: name, color and order them, move, resize and color terminals on them, and add frames. With sessions:write it may rename and tag a terminal, change its fields and give it a color theme. It reaches only the projects its token reaches.
custom.program.agent: The agent in a terminal describes its own terminal and no other: a name, a summary of what it is for, its links and its fields, with aubergine describe, aubergine link add and aubergine field set. Where you wrote a name, a summary or a field yourself, yours stays, and what the agent sent is kept beside it as a suggestion. An agent, or a program with workflows:write, may also propose a color theme with aubergine theme propose: it is drawn nowhere until you have read it under Review, seen it drawn and tried it on the page, and accepted it, and accepting writes its file and chooses nothing.
custom.program.owner: The settings themselves are yours alone. No token, terminal or agent can change them: PUT /v1/settings/appearance answers only the signed-in browser, and appearance.colors, shortcuts and the rest are written by hand in the file.

custom.cmp.a.settings: config.json and Settings, with a JSON Schema for editors
custom.cmp.a.themes: Ten themes, light, dark or as the system; your own as JSON files over one of them; one for a project, for the terminals with a tag and for each terminal; 35 colors by hand, for every theme or one
custom.cmp.a.css: Yes: custom.css in the data folder, with documented hooks
custom.cmp.a.templates: Two, for a terminal's title and a row of the list: text with placeholders such as {state} and {field:Ticket}
custom.cmp.p1: Every tool here keeps its settings in a file, and VS Code, Zed and Windows Terminal also have a screen that writes it, as Aubergine does. In most of them a theme is a file too: JSON in VS Code and Zed, CSS in Obsidian, Lua or TOML in WezTerm, a configuration file in kitty and Ghostty. VS Code, Zed and WezTerm let you change single colors over a theme, as appearance.colors does here.
custom.cmp.p2: They differ most in code. WezTerm's whole configuration is a Lua program, kitty and iTerm2 run your own Python, and Hyper's plugins are JavaScript that wraps its interface; Obsidian and Hyper also take your own CSS. VS Code's extensions have no access to its interface's DOM, and it supports no style sheet of yours; Zed runs extensions as WebAssembly, with capabilities you can restrict. tmux, WezTerm, kitty and iTerm2 build titles and status lines from templates or functions.
custom.cmp.p3: Aubergine today is at the settings end, and one step past it: themes, colors and keys in files that describe themselves, a page that writes part of the settings, templates for what a terminal's title and its row say, and a stylesheet of yours with hooks that are kept stable. It runs none of your code in the page: plugins are on the roadmap, and not built.
custom.cmp.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with any of the tools named on this page. Their names are the trademarks of their owners.
custom.plan.title: What is planned
custom.plan.text: Plugins, your own code in the page, are planned and not built: see the roadmap.
custom.q.terminal.q: Can each terminal have a different color theme?
custom.q.terminal.a: Yes. Theme… in a terminal's menu draws its body in any of the ten themes, whatever the page is drawn in. Terminals with a tag can be given a theme by that tag in Settings, and the others follow the default you set for terminals, or the page.
custom.q.css.q: Can I add my own CSS to Aubergine?
custom.q.css.a: Yes: custom.css in the data folder (aubergine css new writes one to start from). It is linked last on the page, from the first paint, and the hooks it may rely on are listed in docs/hooks.md. Add ?plain to the page's address to see it without.
custom.q.file.a: It is config.json in Aubergine's data folder. aubergine settings path prints where, and the server prints it when it starts.
custom.q.agent.q: Can an agent change how Aubergine looks?
custom.q.agent.a: Not the settings: they are yours alone. An agent can name and describe its own terminal and propose a color theme, which waits for you to read and accept it; a program whose API token allows it can rename, tag and theme terminals, arrange canvases and propose a theme too.
